title: Fractals and spirals: how rough a coast is, and how leaves turn round a plant stem

summary.text: A straight line is one-dimensional and a flat page is two-dimensional, so how can a crinkly drawn coast fall in between? Your child counts the boxes that a straight line and a coast touch as the boxes shrink, and the coast grows by a number between the two. Then a plant stem gives a second puzzle: leaves climb the stem turning by a fraction of a circle, such as two fifths, and these fractions creep towards the golden angle. Along the way your child folds a paper dragon, draws a line that grows without end inside a small page, and learns why a snail's shell keeps the same shape.
summary.art: A crinkly hand-drawn coastline on squared paper beside a potted plant with numbered paper tags on the leaves and a coiled snail shell.

intro.hook: Draw a straight line across a squared page. Now draw a crinkly coast across it. Count the little squares each one touches. Halve the squares and count again. The straight line doubles its count. A filled page would quadruple. What will the coast do?
intro.text: In Class 3 you measured a coast with long and short strips, and you counted the spirals on a pineapple. Now you go one step deeper. You will give a rough edge a number, by counting boxes. You will draw a line that gets longer and longer inside the same small space. You will tag the leaves on a real stem and find how far each leaf turns from the last. At the end you find out what spiral shapes in shells, storms and galaxies have in common, and what they do not.
intro.art: A straight line and a crinkly coast on squared paper, both crossing the same grid, with a small number of squares shaded for each.

outcomes: I can say what happens to a line, a flat shape and a solid when they are made twice as big, and use this to explain what a roughness number means.
I can measure the roughness of a drawn coast by counting the boxes it touches at three box sizes, and say why the answer lies between 1 and 2.
I can build a Koch curve and a paper dragon and explain how repeating one rule makes a fractal.
I can explain why a growing shell keeps the same shape, and tell a spiral that grows by a fraction from one that grows by adding the same amount.
I can find the fraction of a turn between neighbouring leaves on a real stem, and compare it with the fractions 1 over 2, 1 over 3, 2 over 5 and 3 over 8 and with the golden angle.
I can explain why branching helps trees, lungs and blood vessels, and say what is still debated about the rules for branch widths.
I can explain how random walkers build a branching cluster, and say why a shell, a cyclone and a galaxy can each be a spiral for a different reason.

terms.meaning: The size at which you look at or measure something. Changing the scale means making the measuring step or the picture bigger or smaller.
terms.example: A map of India on a page and a map of Chennai on a page are drawn at different scales.
terms.art: Two maps side by side, one of all India and one of a single city, with a ruler beside each.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how a shape's size grows when you make it bigger. A line has dimension 1, a flat page has dimension 2 and a solid block has dimension 3. A rough edge can have a dimension in between.
terms.example: A straight string has dimension 1. A crumpled ball of foil is somewhere between 2 and 3.
terms.art: A line, a flat square and a cube, labelled 1, 2 and 3, with a crumpled ball of foil beside them.

terms.meaning: Another name used in this unit for the dimension of a rough edge, such as a coast. A straight line has roughness number 1 and a very crinkly coast has a roughness number above 1, but always less than 2.
terms.example: The west coast of Britain has a roughness number of about 1.25.
terms.art: A scale from 1 to 2 with a straight line at the left end, a gentle coast in the middle and a very crinkly coast near the right end.

terms.meaning: A way to measure roughness. You cover a drawing with boxes, count the boxes that touch the line, and then repeat with smaller boxes.
terms.example: A straight line touches 5 boxes of 4 centimetres and 10 boxes of 2 centimetres. The count doubles when the boxes halve.
terms.art: A coast drawn on a grid with the squares it passes through shaded.

terms.meaning: Doing the same step again and again, each time on the result of the last. Making a fractal is often iteration of one rule.
terms.example: Folding a paper strip in half, then in half again, then again, is iteration of one fold.
terms.art: A paper strip folded in half three times, with the folds shown one after another.

terms.meaning: A line made by one rule repeated: take every straight piece, cut out its middle third and replace it with two sides of a tent. The line gets longer each time and never stops growing.
terms.example: A 27 centimetre line becomes 36 centimetres after one round and 48 after two.
terms.art: A straight line, then the same line with a tent in the middle third, then with smaller tents on each piece.

terms.meaning: How many times bigger one thing is than another, found by dividing. If one coil is 36 millimetres and the next is 24, the ratio is 36 divided by 24, which is 1.5.
terms.example: A shell whose coils each get 1.5 times wider has a ratio of 1.5 between neighbouring coils.
terms.art: Two bars of different lengths with the longer one labelled 1.5 times the shorter.

terms.meaning: A spiral whose coils are the same distance apart all the way out. It grows by adding the same amount each turn.
terms.example: A coiled rope, a mosquito coil and a murukku are close to Archimedean spirals.
terms.art: A coil of rope seen from above with equal gaps between turns marked by small arrows.

terms.meaning: A spiral whose coils get wider by the same fraction each turn, so the gaps grow bigger and bigger. A logarithmic spiral keeps the same shape as it grows.
terms.example: A snail shell and a nautilus shell are close to logarithmic spirals.
terms.art: A nautilus shell cut in half, with the gaps between coils marked and growing larger outwards.

terms.meaning: One full turn of a coiled shell. A shell is made of a number of whorls, each wider than the one before.
terms.example: A long pointed shell has five or six whorls.
terms.art: A long pointed shell with each whorl marked by a different colour band.

terms.meaning: The way leaves, seeds or petals are arranged round a stem or a seed head. The word comes from Greek words for leaf and arrangement.
terms.example: A stem with leaves that each turn two fifths of a circle round the stem has a phyllotaxis of 2 over 5.
terms.art: A plant stem seen from above with numbered leaves spiralling out from the centre.

terms.meaning: A turn of about 137.5 degrees, a little more than a third of a full circle. Many plants place each new leaf or seed about this far round from the last.
terms.example: Turning two fifths of a circle gives 144 degrees. Turning three eighths gives 135 degrees. Both are close to the golden angle.
terms.art: A circle with a pointer turned 137.5 degrees from a vertical line, with the angle marked.

terms.meaning: A path made of steps in directions chosen by chance, like following a die. A random walker has no goal and does not plan a route.
terms.example: A dust speck jiggled by air moves in a random walk.
terms.art: A zig-zag path across a grid, with an arrow at each step pointing in a different direction.

terms.meaning: A group of things stuck together. In a growth game, a cluster is the set of squares or particles that have joined the seed.
terms.example: The branching shape that builds up when walkers stick to a seed is a cluster.
terms.art: A seed square in the middle of a grid with a branching cluster of shaded squares growing out.

terms.meaning: A huge spinning storm with winds that spiral in towards a calm centre.
terms.example: A cyclone in the Bay of Bengal spins anticlockwise when seen from above.
terms.art: A satellite picture of a cyclone over the Bay of Bengal with spiral arms of cloud.

terms.meaning: The way the spin of the Earth bends the path of air and water that moves over long distances. It turns moving air to the right in the north and to the left in the south.
terms.example: The Coriolis effect makes air rushing into a low-pressure area spiral round it.
terms.art: Arrows of air curving to the right as they rush towards a low-pressure centre in the northern half of the Earth.

terms.meaning: A pattern of spots or stripes made when two chemicals spread through a surface and react, as the mathematician Alan Turing worked out in 1952.
terms.example: Scientists think the stripes on some fish form this way.
terms.art: A fish with stripes, beside a diagram of two chemicals spreading across a surface.

terms.meaning: A curve made by folding a paper strip in half again and again in the same direction and opening each fold to a right angle.
terms.example: A strip folded four times opens into a curve with 15 corners.
terms.art: A paper strip folded in half four times and then opened into a zig-zag curve.

terms.meaning: Looking like itself at different sizes only roughly, not exactly. Real coasts, mountains and clouds are self-similar on average, while a computer fractal can be exactly self-similar.
terms.example: A mountain range looks equally rough up close and from far, but no small part is an exact copy of a large part.
terms.art: A mountain ridge in three zoom levels, each equally jagged but all different.

explanations.concept: What happens to size when a shape doubles
explanations.definition: When a shape is made twice as big in every direction, its length doubles, its area becomes 4 times as big and its volume becomes 8 times as big.
explanations.description: Take a line 5 centimetres long and make it twice as long. It is now 10 centimetres, so it is 2 times as big. Take a square 5 centimetres on each side, with an area of 25 square centimetres. Double each side and the square has an area of 100, which is 4 times as big. Take a cube 5 centimetres on each side, with a volume of 125 cubic centimetres. Double each edge and the volume is 1000, which is 8 times as big. The numbers 2, 4 and 8 are 2 once, twice and three times over. They tell us that a line has dimension 1, a square has dimension 2 and a cube has dimension 3. The dimension is the number of times you multiply 2 by itself to get the growth.
examples: A line: double it, and it grows 2 times.
A square: double its sides, and it grows 4 times.
A cube: double its edges, and it grows 8 times.
A big idli takes in 8 times more batter than one with half the width, if the shapes are the same.
explanations.art: A line, a square and a cube each drawn twice, small and double size, with 2, 4 and 8 written beside them.

explanations.concept: Giving a rough edge a number: box counting
explanations.definition: In box counting, you cover a drawing with boxes, count the boxes that touch the line, then halve the boxes and count again. How fast the count grows tells you how rough the line is.
explanations.description: Use the idea of doubling in reverse. If you halve the size of the boxes that cover a straight line, you need twice as many boxes. If you halve the boxes that cover a filled page, you need 4 times as many. A crinkly coast lies in between. When you halve the boxes, the coast needs more than twice as many, but fewer than 4 times as many. If the count rises by 2.4 times each time, the coast has a roughness number of about 1.3. A coast that is almost straight gives a number close to 1. A coast so crinkly that it nearly fills the page gives a number close to 2. The mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot used Lewis Fry Richardson's measurements to show that the west coast of Britain has a number of about 1.25. This number is called a fractal dimension. It is a measure of roughness, and it can be a fraction.
examples: A straight line: count doubles, number 1.
A filled square: count quadruples, number 2.
A coast whose count rises 2.4 times: number about 1.3.
The west coast of Britain: about 1.25.
explanations.art: Three grids with a straight line, a coast and a filled square, and the count of shaded boxes growing as the boxes shrink.

explanations.concept: A line that gets longer for ever in a small space: the Koch curve
explanations.definition: A Koch curve is made by taking a line, cutting out the middle third of every straight piece and putting in two sides of a tent in its place. Repeated for ever, it makes a line of endless length that fits inside a small page.
explanations.description: Start with a line 27 centimetres long. Cut out the middle third, which is 9 centimetres, and put in two 9 centimetre sides of a tent. Now the line has 4 pieces of 9 centimetres, so its length is 36. Do the same to every piece. Now there are 16 pieces of 3 centimetres, and the length is 48. Each round multiplies the length by 4 over 3. After 5 rounds the line is more than a metre long, and after 10 rounds it is nearly 5 metres, yet it never leaves the page. The Swedish mathematician Helge von Koch described this curve in 1904. If three Koch curves are joined into a triangle, they make the Koch snowflake. The snowflake has an edge that is endless, but its area never grows past 1.6 times the area of the starting triangle. So a shape can have a finite area and an endless edge.
examples: 27 cm, then 36, then 48, then 64: each step multiplies by 4 over 3.
The Koch snowflake: an endless edge around a small area.
A coast: the same kind of bends within bends, though stopping at some size.
explanations.art: A Koch curve in three rounds, with the lengths 27, 36 and 48 written under each.

explanations.concept: One rule repeated: how a few instructions make a fern
explanations.definition: Many fractals are made by iteration, which means repeating one small rule on its own result. A very short set of rules can describe a complicated shape.
explanations.description: The mathematician Michael Barnsley showed in the 1980s that a picture of a fern can be drawn from just four short rules. Each rule says how to move a dot to a new place, and a die decides which rule to use. After a few thousand dots, a fern appears. You can try a simpler version by hand, called the chaos game. Mark three corners of a triangle. Put a dot anywhere. Roll a die to choose a corner, and move halfway to that corner. Put a new dot there. Repeat. The dots do not fill the triangle. They build the Sierpinski triangle, a triangle with triangular holes inside holes. Chance chooses where each dot goes, but the rule makes the shape come out the same every time. A computer can store a fern in a few numbers, while a photograph of a fern needs millions.
examples: The chaos game with a die and three corners: the Sierpinski triangle.
A fern drawn by four rules and thousands of dots.
Folding a paper strip again and again: the dragon curve.
explanations.art: A triangle with dots placed by dice, with holes appearing in the middle, next to a computer-drawn fern.

explanations.concept: Why branches get thinner by a rule
explanations.description: Leonardo da Vinci noticed that when a tree branch splits, the areas of the cut ends of the daughter branches add up to the area of the cut end of the mother branch. So the cut ends of all the branches at one height add up to about the trunk. Blood vessels follow a different rule, found by Cecil Murray in 1926. For vessels, the cubes of the widths add up. Both rules help the living body move fluid at the least cost. But why trees follow Leonardo's rule is not settled.
examples: A tree: the cut ends of all the branches at one height add up to about the trunk.
A blood vessel splitting in two: two equal daughter vessels are each about 80 percent as wide as the mother vessel.
A river: each tributary adds to the main river.

perspectives.explanation: A tree has to carry water from the roots to all the leaves. If the total width of the pipes stays the same at every height, the water can flow up evenly. This idea, called the pipe model, was put forward by Japanese botanists in the 1960s.

In 2011 the scientist Christophe Eloy showed that Leonardo's rule fits a tree whose branches, big and small, are about equally likely to snap in the wind. So a tree built this way is equally safe against wind at every size. Both explanations may be partly right.

explanations.art: A tree split into branches with their widths marked, next to a blood vessel splitting into two thinner vessels.

explanations.concept: Real fractals are rough copies, over a limited range of sizes
explanations.definition: A mathematical fractal repeats exactly for ever. A real coast, tree or cloud repeats only on average, and only between a biggest and a smallest size.
explanations.description: The Koch curve is exact: a small piece is a perfect copy of a bigger piece. A real coast is not. No small bay is an exact copy of a big gulf. But if you zoom in and out, the coast looks about as rough at every size. Scientists call this being self-similar on average. A real fern repeats its leaflets for only three or four levels. A real coast stops being rough at the grains of sand. So the roughness number you measure with boxes is only true for the range of box sizes you used. Your drawn coast has only three levels of detail, so the number you find is a rough guess, but it is still a useful number for comparing coasts. Doctors use similar numbers to describe how branched a lung or a blood supply is.
examples: A mountain ridge: equally rough close up and far away, but no exact copies.
A fern: leaflets on leaflets for three or four levels.
A drawn coast: three levels of detail, so a rough number.
explanations.art: A mountain ridge drawn at three zoom levels, with the same roughness at each.

explanations.concept: Spirals that keep their shape: shells
explanations.definition: A shell grows by making each new whorl a fixed fraction wider than the last. That is a logarithmic spiral, and the shell keeps the same shape as it grows.
explanations.description: A rope coiled on the floor has equal gaps between its turns. It grows by adding the same amount each turn, and it is called an Archimedean spiral. A snail shell is different. Each new whorl is wider than the last by the same fraction, say 1.5 times. So the gaps get bigger and bigger. This is a logarithmic spiral. Because the fraction is always the same, a small shell and a big shell of one kind have the same shape, and you can work out the missing small whorls of a broken shell by dividing. In the 1960s, the palaeontologist David Raup showed that four numbers are enough to describe the shape of most coiled shells: how fast the whorls widen, how far the opening sits from the middle, how fast the shell slides along its axis, and the shape of the opening. The mathematician Jacob Bernoulli loved the logarithmic spiral so much that it is said he asked for one on his tombstone. The stonemason carved a different kind.
examples: A coiled rope: equal gaps, Archimedean.
A snail shell: growing gaps, logarithmic.
A broken shell: divide each whorl by the fraction to find the missing whorls.
The nautilus: a chambered shell whose spiral is close to logarithmic.
explanations.art: A coiled rope with equal gaps beside a snail shell cut in half with gaps growing outward.

explanations.concept: How plants turn their leaves: fractions and the golden angle
explanations.definition: Leaves climb a stem turning by a fixed fraction of a circle between neighbours. The fractions 1 over 2, 1 over 3, 2 over 5, 3 over 8 and 5 over 13 are common, and they get closer and closer to the golden angle of 137.5 degrees.
explanations.description: Look at a stem from above. If each leaf turns half a circle from the last, the leaves stack in just two rows, and the ones in the same row shade each other. If each turns a third, they stack in three rows. A turn of two fifths, 144 degrees, gives five rows before leaves repeat. A turn of three eighths, 135 degrees, gives eight rows. Each of these fractions is a Fibonacci number over the next-but-one Fibonacci number, such as 2 over 5 and 3 over 8. The next fractions in the list are 5 over 13, which is 138.5 degrees, 8 over 21, which is 137.1 degrees, and 13 over 34, which is 137.65 degrees. They close in on 137.5 degrees, the golden angle. The golden angle is the turn that never lines a leaf up exactly above an earlier leaf, however many leaves there are. It is the turn that is furthest of all from every simple fraction. A plant with a turn near the golden angle spreads leaves into many rows, so every leaf gets light. The brothers Auguste and Louis Bravais measured the angle in the 1830s.
examples: Half a turn: two rows of leaves, as in many grasses.
A third: three rows.
Two fifths, 144 degrees: five rows.
Three eighths, 135 degrees: eight rows.
explanations.art: A plant stem seen from above, with leaf 0 to leaf 8 numbered along a spiral, and a circle marked with turns of 144 and 135 degrees.

explanations.description: A cyclone is a spiral, but for a very different reason from a shell. Air rushes in towards a low-pressure centre. Because the Earth spins, the moving air is bent by the Coriolis effect, to the right in the north and to the left in the south. So a cyclone in the Bay of Bengal spins anticlockwise when seen from above. A galaxy such as the Milky Way has spiral arms of stars and gas. Scientists think the arms are waves of squeezing that move through the stars, like a traffic jam moving along a road while the cars come and go. This idea, the density wave theory, was put forward by C. C. Lin and Frank Shu in 1964. It is not the only explanation, and how galaxy arms last is still an open question. So the same spiral shape in a shell, a storm and a galaxy comes from three different causes. A shape does not tell you why it is there.
examples: A shell: each whorl wider by a fixed fraction.
A cyclone: moving air bent by the Earth's spin.
A galaxy: probably waves of squeezing in the stars and gas.
explanations.art: A shell, a satellite picture of a cyclone and a galaxy, side by side, each with a one-line cause beneath.

explanations.concept: Spots and stripes from chemicals that spread
explanations.description: In 1952 the mathematician Alan Turing worked out how an even, featureless surface could make spots or stripes by itself. He imagined two chemicals that spread through the skin and react with each other. One makes more of both. The other spreads faster and stops the first. The result is a pattern with a set spacing between spots. Turing patterns are well studied on a computer. They have been found in real animals in some cases. In 1995, Shigeru Kondo and Rihito Asai saw stripes on the marine angelfish slowly move and split into new stripes, as the model predicts. How general the idea is for animals such as leopards and zebras is still debated.
examples: Stripes of the marine angelfish, which move and split as the fish grows.
Spots of a leopard, which may follow a Turing rule.
The evenly spaced fingers of a mouse paw, which have been linked to a Turing-type process.

perspectives.explanation: The patterns on some fish, and the spacing of fingers, match the model's predictions, and experiments that change one chemical change the pattern in the way the model says.

A model that makes the right picture is not proof that the animal uses the same process. Many animal patterns may come from other mixes of signals, and the chemicals have only been found in a few cases.

explanations.art: A fish with stripes beside two small maps showing one chemical spreading slowly and another spreading fast.

explanations.definition: When particles wander at random and stick to a growing cluster at the first place they touch it, the cluster grows branches. The tips catch most of the walkers, so the tips grow fastest.
explanations.description: Imagine a seed in the middle of a table and a dust speck wandering at random. When the speck touches the seed, the speck sticks. Then another speck wanders in and sticks to the cluster. A speck wandering in from far away is most likely to bump into a tip that sticks out, before it ever reaches a hollow between two arms. So the tips catch more walkers, and they grow further out. That makes the cluster branch, with bumps becoming arms and bumps on the arms becoming smaller arms. In 1981, the physicists Thomas Witten and Leonard Sander worked this out and called it diffusion-limited aggregation. The same kind of growth makes the branching crystals of copper in some chemical cells, the black fern-like marks of manganese in rocks and parts of the branching in lightning. The rule says nothing about ferns or lightning. It only says that tips catch more.
examples: The paper game with a die and a seed square.
Fern-like dark marks on some rocks, caused by minerals.
The branches of lightning.
explanations.art: A grid with a seed in the middle and walkers drawn as dotted paths, with a branched cluster in the centre.

explanations.concept: Fractals made by people: antennas, art and villages
explanations.definition: People use fractal shapes because a fractal packs a very long edge into a small space. Some artists and builders have also used repeating rules at several sizes.
explanations.description: A radio antenna works by having a long wire. A fractal antenna folds a long wire into a repeating pattern that fits in a small space, so it can catch several wavelengths at once. The engineer Nathan Cohen built fractal antennas from the late 1980s, and they have been tested for phones and other devices. Kolam makers and temple builders have used repeating patterns at several sizes for centuries. The scholar Ron Eglash said in 1999 that many villages in Africa were built as fractals, with houses, streets and lanes repeating in rings at several sizes. Some researchers agree that the patterns are real, and some say he went too far in saying the builders planned a fractal. Whether a pattern was planned or just grew is a question worth asking each time.
examples: A fractal antenna folded into a small chip.
A kolam with loops inside loops.
Village layouts with rings of houses of different sizes.
explanations.art: A small square antenna with a long folded wire in a repeating pattern, a kolam with loops inside loops and a ring-shaped village from above.

agreed.text: A line has dimension 1, a flat shape has dimension 2 and a solid has dimension 3, and a rough edge such as a coast can have a dimension between 1 and 2.
agreed.evidence: You can measure it by box counting. Mandelbrot used Richardson's measurements to give the west coast of Britain about 1.25.

agreed.text: A Koch curve gets 4 over 3 times longer with each round, so it grows without end, yet it fits inside a small page.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can draw the first two rounds and measure them. The pattern in the lengths, 27, 36, 48, 64, can be checked by arithmetic.

agreed.text: A coiled shell grows by making each whorl a fixed fraction wider than the last, so the shell keeps the same shape.
agreed.evidence: Scientists such as David Raup showed that four numbers describe the shape of most coiled shells, and growth lines on shells match the pattern.

agreed.text: Leaves on many plants turn by a fraction of a circle such as 1 over 2, 1 over 3, 2 over 5 or 3 over 8 between neighbours, and these fractions approach the golden angle of about 137.5 degrees.
agreed.evidence: Botanists have counted leaf turns for nearly two hundred years, and anyone with a plant can check by tagging leaves.

agreed.text: Cyclones spiral because the spinning Earth bends the path of air rushing in to a low-pressure centre.
agreed.evidence: Cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the northern half of the Earth and clockwise in the southern half, as the Coriolis effect predicts.

agreed.text: When walkers wander at random and stick at first touch, the tips of the cluster catch the most walkers, and the cluster grows branches.
agreed.evidence: Witten and Sander showed it in a computer in 1981, and anyone can repeat it with a die and a grid.

challenging.claim: A coast has one true roughness number, like its length in kilometres.
challenging.who: Some who first read about fractal coasts.
challenging.for: Richardson and Mandelbrot found that the west coast of Britain gives a number of about 1.25 over a wide range of sizes.
challenging.against: A real coast is only rough on average over a range of sizes, and different stretches and different ranges give different numbers. The number depends on how and where it is measured.

challenging.claim: Water drains from a sink in opposite directions in the northern and southern halves of the Earth.
challenging.who: A popular story told to tourists and in some schools.
challenging.for: Cyclones really do spin in opposite directions in the two halves.
challenging.against: The Coriolis effect is far too weak at the size of a sink. The direction of the swirl is set by the shape of the sink and the way the water was stirred. Cyclones are huge, and that is why the Earth's spin matters to them.

challenging.claim: Many African villages were built as fractals by design.
challenging.who: Ron Eglash, in 1999, and many who have read his work.
challenging.for: Aerial photographs of some villages show rings of houses and lanes that repeat at several sizes.
challenging.against: Some researchers say that the evidence that builders planned the fractal is weak, and that a pattern can appear from simple rules of growth without a plan.

challenging.claim: The golden ratio is behind the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and many other great works of art.
challenging.for: Rectangles close to the golden ratio can be drawn over pictures of those works.
challenging.against: Measurements of the works do not match well, and you can draw a golden rectangle over almost anything. There is no record that most of the artists used it.

challenging.claim: The spots and stripes of animals such as leopards and zebras are made by a Turing process.
challenging.who: Many biologists, with evidence from a few animals.
challenging.for: Turing patterns give the right kind of spots and stripes, and have been seen in angelfish and in mouse fingers.
challenging.against: The model's picture is not proof of the process. For most animals, nobody has found the two chemicals or tested the model.

big_questions.q: Your coast came out at a roughness number between 1 and 2. Can something have a size that is not a whole number?
big_questions.hint: A line has size 1 and a page has size 2. What would a thing that is more than a line and less than a page be like?

big_questions.q: A snail keeps adding shell by the same fraction. Does a snail know the shape she is building, or is the shape just what the repeated step makes?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether knowing the shape is needed to make the shape.

big_questions.q: Leaves turn by about 137.5 degrees from one to the next. How does a plant end up with a number like that?
big_questions.hint: The number may come out of a simple rule about gaps. What rule might that be?

big_questions.q: A shell, a cyclone and a galaxy are all spirals, for different reasons. Does a shared shape mean a shared cause?
big_questions.hint: Think of two different foods that are both round. Do they have to be made the same way?

big_questions.q: The Koch snowflake has an endless edge and a small area. Can you hold infinity in your hand?
big_questions.hint: You can draw the first rounds. What would the next ones look like? Where does the drawing stop being possible?

big_questions.q: If a coast has no single length, who should decide how a border or a coast is measured, and does it matter?
big_questions.hint: Think about fishing rights, taxes, disputes between countries and maps made for different jobs.

big_questions.q: Trees, lungs, rivers and lightning all branch. Why does the same shape solve so many different problems?
big_questions.hint: What does each one need to reach or collect?

big_questions.q: The stripes on some fish form from chemicals spreading. Is a fish's pattern planned, or does the pattern just happen?
big_questions.hint: Is there a difference between a plan and a rule that gives the same result every time?

story.title: The Shell That Remembered
story.note: A made-up story. Shell stalls near Rameswaram, long pointed shells with whorls, and growth by a fixed fraction are real. The three measurements and the whole shell are imagined, and real shells widen at their own rate.
text: Revathi spent every May holiday at her uncle's shell stall near the Pamban bridge, in Rameswaram. Murugan Maama sold shells to the tourists. There were pink conches, speckled cowries, and long pointed shells that wound up like screws.
Revathi liked the pointed ones best. She had noticed something. A baby shell and a big shell of the same kind looked exactly alike. The big one was only bigger.
'Big shell, old snail,' said Maama, waving a hand. 'Small shell, young snail. That's all there is to know.'

One morning, a woman with a canvas bag stopped at the stall. She said her name was Dr. Fathima, and that she studied sea snails at a university in Chennai. She picked up a long pointed shell with a broken tip.
'The net of a fishing boat brought this up from deep water,' she said. 'This kind is rare. But the tip is missing. I want to know how many tiny coils it once had, and how big they were.'
'That tip is gone for ever,' said Maama. 'Better to buy a whole one.'
'A whole one is not the same shell,' said Dr. Fathima, smiling.
Revathi looked at the broken shell. 'Maybe we can work it out,' she said.
Maama laughed. Dr. Fathima did not. 'How?' she asked.
'The small shells look like the big shells,' said Revathi. 'So the snail must grow by a rule. If we find the rule, we can go backwards.'
'Good thinking,' said Dr. Fathima. 'Here is a question. Does the snail add the same amount each time, like a rope coiling up? Or does she make each coil the same fraction bigger?'
Revathi fetched a coil of rope from behind the stall and laid it flat. She held her school ruler across the middle. The gaps between the turns of the rope were all the same, about two fingers wide.
'The rope adds the same amount,' she said. 'Now the shell.'
She held the ruler across the broken shell and measured the widths of the last three whorls. They were 36 millimetres, 24 millimetres and 16 millimetres.

'Thirty-six take away twenty-four is twelve,' she said. 'Twenty-four take away sixteen is eight. Not the same.' She frowned. Then she tried dividing. 'Thirty-six divided by twenty-four is one and a half. Twenty-four divided by sixteen is one and a half!'

'Each coil is one and a half times the one before,' said Dr. Fathima. 'The snail does not add the same amount. She makes each new coil the same fraction bigger. That is why her shell never changes shape.'

'Then I can go backwards,' said Revathi. She divided sixteen by one and a half, and got about eleven. Eleven divided by one and a half was about seven. Seven divided by one and a half was about five. Five divided by one and a half was about three.
She drew five coils in her notebook, with widths of 3, 5, 7, 11 and 16 millimetres. They curled together into a tiny tip.

Dr. Fathima reached into her canvas bag and took out a small plastic box. Inside lay a very small shell of the same kind, a young snail's, from a museum drawer. Revathi held her drawing up beside it. The baby shell's coils, from the tip, were about 3, 5, 7 and 11 millimetres.
Maama stared at the drawing, and then at the baby shell. 'It's the same,' he said.
'It's a rule, not luck,' said Revathi. 'The shell remembers every size the snail has been.'
'But how does the snail know about one and a half?' asked Maama.
'No one has watched a snail count,' said Dr. Fathima. 'Her body keeps making the new edge a little wider than the last. Scientists are still finding out exactly how.'

Dr. Fathima bought the broken shell, and she asked if she could keep Revathi's drawing. The next morning Maama lined his shells up from the smallest to the biggest, and propped a card against the row. It said, in careful handwriting, 'Ask Revathi: what was the shell like when it was small?'
story.epiphany: A shell grows by making each new coil the same fraction bigger than the last, not the same amount bigger. From any three coils you can divide to find the smaller coils before them, even those of a broken tip.
ask: Why did dividing work for the shell when taking away did not?
If the widest whorl is 54 millimetres and each whorl is 1.5 times the one before, how wide was the whorl before it?
What is a difference between the way a rope coils and the way a shell coils?
Where else might you use a rule to work backwards from what is left?

roots.context: We have given a rough coast a number, grown a line without end inside a page, and tagged leaves that turn by a fraction of a circle. Now we ask what these patterns tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A straight line doubles its boxes when the boxes are halved. A filled page quadruples them. Your coast went up by about 2.4 times, in between. So a rough edge has a size between a line and a page.
deep_truth.habit: We sort every shape into a line, a flat sheet or a solid, and think its size must be 1, 2 or 3. A rough edge shows that this is a habit of our rulers and not a rule of nature.
deep_truth.evidence: In the box test, a straight line went from 5 to 10 to 20 boxes, doubling each time the boxes were halved. Your coast went up by about 2.4 times each time, which gives a roughness number near 1.3. If your numbers differ, write them down as they are.

three.who_am_i: Your blood vessels split again and again, by a rule about their widths that Cecil Murray described in 1926. Your body is full of branches that follow a pattern.
three.what_is_life: A plant turns each new leaf by a fraction of a circle, such as two fifths, so that her leaves share the light. A snail makes each new coil a fixed fraction bigger. Each repeats a single step.
three.what_is_this_world: A shell, a cyclone and a galaxy are all spirals, for three different reasons. A shape in the world can come from many different causes.

roots.thread: A Koch curve starts as a straight line, and one rule repeated makes an endless crinkly edge. A fern can be drawn from four rules and a die. A snail builds a shell by repeating one fraction, and a plant turns each leaf by one fraction of a circle. In each case, one simple step done again and again makes a rich shape. The many shapes of the world can come from a very few steps, repeated.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to split the seed of a banyan fruit and say what he sees inside. Shvetaketu sees nothing. Uddalaka says that the fine part you cannot see is the reason the great banyan tree stands.
teachings.link: A tree with thousands of branches grows from a seed, and the whole branching pattern comes from a few simple steps repeated. Nothing in the seed looks like a tree.

teachings.source: William Blake, Auguries of Innocence, opening lines
teachings.teaching: To see a World in a Grain of Sand, and a Heaven in a Wild Flower, hold Infinity in the palm of your hand, and Eternity in an hour.
teachings.link: A Koch curve of endless length fits in the palm of your hand, and zooming in on a coast finds new bends at each size.

science.text: Using Richardson's measurements, Benoit Mandelbrot showed in 1967 that the west coast of Britain behaves as if it has a roughness number of about 1.25.
How the spiral arms of a galaxy last for billions of years is still being studied. The density wave idea is one explanation, and there are others.

other_view.view: The roughness number you measure from a drawing or a map holds only between a smallest and a largest box size. Beyond those sizes a coast is no longer rough in the same way. So calling a coast a fractal is a useful way of describing it, and it is not a deep fact about the world.

practice.title: Out to the tips, back to the trunk
practice.say: Look at a tree through a window. Breathe in slowly as your eyes follow the trunk up to a big branch. Keep breathing in as they follow it to a smaller branch and then a twig. Breathe out as your eyes come back down to the trunk. Do this three times. Where does a branch end and the tree begin?
practice.kid: Look at a tree. Follow it with your eyes from trunk to twig. Breathe in on the way out. Breathe out on the way back.

ask: Your coast measured about 1.3, between a line and a page. What else might we have sorted into boxes too neatly?
A plant turns each leaf by a fraction of a circle, and the fractions close in on 137.5 degrees. Is the pattern in the plant, in the rule, or in our counting?
A snail shell, a cyclone and a galaxy are all spirals. Are they one pattern or three?

games.title: Stick and Wander: grow a branching cluster with a die
games.context: This is a game of chance that builds a shape. You release walkers that wander at random and stick to a seed, and a branching cluster grows on your grid.

setup.art: A 7 by 7 grid of squares on paper with the middle square shaded, a bean standing on a square on the top edge and a die beside the sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Take a grid sheet. The shaded middle square is the seed. Put a bean on the edge for the walker.

setup.art: A bean walking one square at a time across the grid with small arrows for up, right, down and left matching the numbers 1 to 4 on a die.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die for each step. 1 is up, 2 is right, 3 is down, 4 is left.

setup.art: A grid where the walker has landed next to the seed and the square has been shaded and numbered 1, with a branching cluster after several more walkers.
setup.caption: 3. When the walker touches the cluster, shade its square and write its number.

printables.title: 3 grid sheets: each a 7 by 7 grid of squares with the middle square shaded as the seed
items: Grid sheet for round 1: 7 by 7 squares, middle square shaded
Grid sheet for round 2: 7 by 7 squares, middle square shaded
Grid sheet for round 3: 7 by 7 squares, middle square shaded

printables.title: 1 score sheet: for each round, the number of walkers needed to reach the edge
items: Round 1: walkers used to reach the edge
Round 2: walkers used to reach the edge
Round 3: walkers used to reach the edge

rules: Each player has a grid sheet with the middle square shaded. The shaded square is the seed. Each player needs a marker, such as a bean or a button, for the walker, and ideally a die of their own (a ludo die will do). Everyone plays at the same time on their own sheet. If there is only one die, pass it on each time a walker sticks. No die: toss two coins for each step instead (two heads is up, head and tail is right, tail and head is down, two tails is left), so no toss is wasted.
To release a walker, roll the die to pick an edge: 1 is the top edge, 2 the right edge, 3 the bottom edge and 4 the left edge. On a 5 or 6, roll again.

Roll again to pick the starting square on that edge. Count that many squares from the left for the top or bottom edge, or from the top for the side edges (a 6 means the last, seventh square). Put the marker there. If it starts next to the cluster, it sticks at once.

Move the walker one square at a time. For each step, roll the die: 1 is up, 2 is right, 3 is down and 4 is left. On a 5 or 6, roll again. If the step would take the walker off the grid, the walker stays where it is.

A walker sticks as soon as it is next to a shaded square, sharing a side. Touching only at a corner does not count. Shade the square the walker is on and write its number in it. The first walker is 1, the second is 2, and so on.

Take turns. On your turn, release one walker and walk it until it sticks. A round ends when a cluster has a shaded square on the edge of the sheet. The player who reaches the edge first wins the round. If a round has gone on for more than 10 minutes, stop it when a cluster has 9 shaded squares, and count the winner as the one with the most squares on the outer ring.
Play up to 3 rounds, one on each sheet. Two rounds are enough if time is short. The player who wins the most rounds wins the game. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone: release walkers until the cluster reaches the edge, and count how many walkers it took. Play two or three rounds and try to beat your best.

flow.do: Print or draw the 3 grid sheets. Shade the middle square on each. Give each player a marker. Put one die in the middle.
flow.say: Each of you has a grid and a seed in the middle. A walker will wander in from the edge and stick to the seed. Let us see what shape grows.
flow.kid: Shade the middle square. Get a bean. Get a die.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stick and Wander. You set up the grids, the markers and the die.

flow.do: Play the first few walkers. Release a walker, roll to pick its edge and its square, and walk it until it sticks. Shade and number the square.
flow.say: Roll to choose the edge. Roll again for the square. Now roll for each step. When the walker is next to a shaded square, it sticks. Shade its square.
flow.kid: Roll to pick the edge. Roll for each step. When it touches, shade it.
flow.parent: Typical numbers, not promises: a walker needs about 10 to 80 steps before it sticks, so 15 to 120 rolls, and the first walkers are the slowest. A round usually needs about 6 to 12 walkers and 100 to 400 rolls, which is 5 to 10 minutes. That is normal; nothing is wrong. A walker that wanders off the grid stays put, so every walker eventually sticks. Beans and buttons are small parts: keep them away from little brothers and sisters, and use buttons or paper squares if anyone has a food allergy to beans. Two to four children can each play their own sheet side by side; one child with a parent can race the parent.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first turns and learn the rules.

flow.do: Keep playing until one cluster has a shaded square on the edge. Write the number of walkers used on the score sheet.
flow.say: Keep going. Who will reach the edge first? Write down how many walkers it took.
flow.kid: Keep playing. See who reaches the edge first.

ask.q: What shape is your cluster growing into?
good: Arms sticking out from the seed.
Branches like a tree.
A star shape.

flow.context: In this step, you play the rest of round 1 until a cluster reaches the edge.

flow.do: Look at the finished clusters. Ask where the walkers stuck: at the end of arms, or in the hollows between arms. Mark the tips with a pencil dot.
flow.say: Look at the cluster. Which numbers are at the tips of arms? Which are in the hollows between arms? Where did walkers stick most?
flow.kid: Look at your cluster. Mark the tips with a dot. Where do walkers stick most?

ask.q: Why did more walkers stick to the tips than to the hollows?
good: A walker coming from outside meets a tip first.
The hollows are hidden between the arms.
The tips stick out.

check.q: Why do the arms of the cluster keep growing longer?
options: A wandering walker is most likely to bump into a tip before it reaches a hollow
Walkers are pulled towards the arms
check.why: A walker wandering in from outside meets the squares that stick out first. Those squares catch the most walkers, so they grow. Hollows between arms are hidden, so few walkers reach them. The die has no pull towards anything.

flow.context: In this step, you look at where the walkers stuck and why the cluster branches.

flow.do: Play round 2, and round 3 if there is time (a second sitting is fine). Write the walker counts on the score sheet. Add up the rounds won and name the winner.
flow.say: Play another round, or two. Is each cluster the same? Is each the same kind of shape?
flow.kid: Play round 2, and round 3 if there is time. Count the walkers. Is each shape the same?

ask.q: Were the three clusters exactly the same?
good: No, but they were the same kind of shape.
No. Each had arms, but in different places.

flow.parent: Every cluster is different because the dice are random. All of them have arms with sub-branches. The kind of shape is the same each time, and the exact shape is not.
flow.context: In this step, you play the later rounds and compare the shapes.

experiments.title: How Rough Is Your Coast? Count the boxes it touches
experiments.question: When the boxes that cover a line are cut in half, how fast does the number of boxes touched grow? Does a crinkly coast grow like a straight line, like a filled page, or in between?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. A straight line touches 5 boxes of 4 centimetres. How many will it touch when the boxes are 2 centimetres? Will your crinkly coast grow by more, less or the same as the straight line? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Draw the straight line and the coast on pages of the same size, 20 centimetres across. Work alone with a parent, or in a group of 2 to 4 where each child draws a coast. Use the same rule for counting a box every time: a box counts if the line passes through any part of it. Count each box size twice. Only the box size changes, so any difference in how fast the count grows comes from the line and not from the counting.
results_table: Boxes touched by the straight line
Coast ratio: this count divided by the count for boxes twice as big

materials.item: 2 sheets of 1 centimetre squared paper (graph paper from a stationery shop, a few rupees a sheet) for each child. If your squares are 5 millimetres, colour every second line first to make 1 centimetre boxes
a sharp pencil and an eraser
a 30 centimetre ruler
2 coloured pencils or pens, one for the 4 centimetre lines and one for the 2 centimetre lines
a pencil and scrap paper for dividing, or a calculator
the lookup table for roughness numbers, written out in step 6

experiments.safety: Sharpen pencils with a grown-up, or use a sharpener with a cover.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick your straight line and your coast in your notebook. Write the roughness number you found, and the word line, in between, or page for how it compares.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you draw a straight line and a crinkly coast on squared paper and count the boxes they touch at three box sizes. You use the counts to give your coast a roughness number.

setup.art: A page of 1 centimetre squares with a straight horizontal line drawn through the middle of a row of squares, from the left edge to the right edge.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a straight line 20 centimetres long through the middle of a row of squares.

setup.art: A second page with a crinkly coast across it, with big bays, smaller bays inside them and tiny wiggles on those.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a crinkly coast across the second page. Add bays inside bays.

setup.art: The same coast with thick coloured lines marking boxes 4 centimetres wide, and the boxes the coast passes through shaded.
setup.caption: 3. Mark boxes 4 centimetres wide. Shade each box the coast passes through.

setup.art: The same coast with boxes 2 centimetres wide and then 1 centimetre wide, with more shaded boxes each time.
setup.caption: 4. Do it again with boxes 2 centimetres wide, and then 1 centimetre wide.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess and give a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table. Then show them a squared page.
flow.say: A straight line touches 5 boxes when the boxes are 4 centimetres wide. How many will it touch when the boxes are half as wide? What will a crinkly coast do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A line touches 5 big boxes. How many small boxes will it touch? What about a crinkly coast?

ask.q: Will the coast's count grow by more than the line's, less, or the same? Why?
good: More, because the coast has more bends to go through.
The same, because both are lines.
Less, because the line is straight and goes through every box.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the box counting test. You guess before you count.

flow.do: On page 1, draw a straight line through the middle of a row of squares. Make it 20 centimetres long. Do not draw it along a grid line. On page 2, draw a coast from the left edge to the right edge. First draw 4 big bays and points. Then add smaller bays on those. Then add tiny wiggles.
flow.say: The straight line goes through the middle of a row, not along a grid line. For the coast, start with big bays. Then put smaller bays inside them. Then even smaller ones. Make it as crinkly as you can.
flow.kid: Draw a straight line in a row of squares. Draw a crinkly coast on page two. Add bays inside bays.
flow.parent: A coast with bays inside bays gives a better result than a smooth wobbly line. Keep the coast from crossing itself. Keep the pencil line thin so the shaded boxes are easy to see.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the straight line and the crinkly coast.

flow.do: On each page, go over every fourth grid line with the first colour. These lines make boxes 4 centimetres wide. Then go over every second line with the second colour. These lines make boxes 2 centimetres wide.
flow.say: Every fourth line makes big boxes. Every second line makes medium boxes. The plain lines make the small boxes.
flow.kid: Colour every fourth line. Colour every second line in another colour.
flow.parent: On a 20 centimetre page, the 4 centimetre grid has 5 boxes across. The 2 centimetre grid has 10. The 1 centimetre grid has 20.
flow.context: In this step, you mark the boxes of three sizes on both pages.

flow.do: On page 1, count the boxes the straight line touches. Do the 4 centimetre boxes first, then the 2 centimetre boxes, then the 1 centimetre boxes. Write the three counts in the table.
flow.say: Count the boxes the straight line touches. Start with the biggest boxes. Then the medium. Then the small. What do you notice about the numbers?
flow.kid: Count the boxes the line touches. Do it for each box size.

ask.q: What happened to the count each time the boxes were halved?
good: It doubled.
It went up by 2 times each time.

check.q: A straight line touches 7 boxes. The boxes are cut to half their width. How many boxes does the line touch now?
check.why: A straight line has dimension 1, so halving the boxes doubles the count. 7 doubled is 14. A filled page would quadruple it to 28.

flow.context: In this step, you count boxes for the straight line and see how fast the count grows.

flow.do: On page 2, count the boxes the coast touches. Do the 4 centimetre boxes first, then the 2 centimetre boxes, then the 1 centimetre boxes. Shade each box as you count it. Count each size twice. Write the counts in the table.
flow.say: Now the coast. Shade each box the coast touches, so you do not count one twice. Start with the biggest boxes. Count twice.
flow.kid: Count the boxes the coast touches. Shade each one. Do it for each box size.
flow.parent: For a coast about 20 centimetres across with bays inside bays, typical counts are 10 to 14 for the 4 centimetre boxes, 25 to 35 for the 2 centimetre boxes, and 60 to 90 for the 1 centimetre boxes. Your own counts may differ. If your two counts of the same size differ by 2 or 3, use the average. With a parent, let the parent do the second count, and compare. With 2 to 4 children, swap coasts and let a friend do the second count; if the friend's numbers differ by more than 3, count the box again together.
flow.context: In this step, you count the boxes your coast touches at three box sizes.

flow.do: Work out the ratios. Divide the 2 centimetre count by the 4 centimetre count. Divide the 1 centimetre count by the 2 centimetre count. Take the middle of the two answers. Then read the roughness number from the table. A ratio of 2.0 gives 1.0. A ratio of 2.2 gives 1.1. A ratio of 2.4 gives 1.3. A ratio of 2.6 gives 1.4. A ratio of 2.8 gives 1.5. A ratio of 3.0 gives 1.6. A ratio of 3.5 gives 1.8. A ratio of 4.0 gives 2.0.
flow.say: Divide each count by the one before. That tells you how many times the count grows when the boxes halve. Find the middle of your two answers. Now look it up in the table.
flow.kid: Divide the counts. Find the middle ratio. Look up your roughness number.

ask.q: Is your coast's ratio nearer to 2, to 4, or in between?
good: In between.
A bit more than 2.
Closer to 2 than to 4.

flow.parent: A line gives a ratio of 2, which is roughness number 1. A filled page gives a ratio of 4, which is number 2. If your ratio is about 2.4, your coast is about 1.3. A hand drawn coast usually lands between 1.1 and 1.5. If your ratio is below 2, you probably missed boxes. Count again. If the second ratio (1 centimetre over 2 centimetre) is smaller than the first, that is normal: your pencil line has run out of fine detail at 1 centimetre. This is why a roughness number is only true for the box sizes you used. Compare the numbers of friends: they will not match exactly.
flow.think: If you drew a smooth coast with only two or three gentle curves, what ratio would you expect?
flow.context: In this step, you turn your counts into a roughness number for your coast.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found. Write the claim, the evidence and the reason.
flow.say: What did you find? What numbers show it? Why do you think the coast grew faster than the line but slower than a filled page?
flow.kid: What did you find? Which numbers show it? Why?

ask.q: Why did the coast's count grow faster than the line's, but slower than a page's?
good: The coast has bends, so it needs more boxes than a straight line.
It does not fill the page, so it needs fewer boxes than a filled page.

flow.parent: A strong answer says: the line's count doubles, the filled page's would quadruple, and the coast's grew by about 2.4 times, in between. The reasoning is that a crinkly line has more to cover than a straight one, but it does not fill the whole page. The number between 1 and 2 describes how much it fills.

check.q: A coast's box count grows by 3.0 times each time the boxes are halved. What can you say about the coast?
options: It is much rougher than a straight line and nearer to filling a page, with a roughness number about 1.6
It is exactly a filled page
check.why: A ratio of 3.0 is between 2 for a line and 4 for a page, and nearer the page. The table gives 1.6. A straight line would give 2.0 and a filled page 4.0.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and why the coast grew in between a line and a page.

experiments.title: Leaf Staircase: how far does each leaf turn round the stem?
experiments.question: As leaves climb a stem, how much does each new leaf turn round the stem from the last one? Is it the same for every plant?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many leaves up the stem before you find one directly above the first? Will each leaf turn half a circle, a third, or something else? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same method on every stem: tag the leaves from the bottom, find the first leaf directly above the bottom one, count the leaves and follow a thread round the stem to count the turns. Count each stem twice, starting from a different leaf the second time, because one count can be wrong. Only the plant changes. With one child, the parent does the second count. With 2 to 4 children, each child takes a different plant: one holds the thread and one reads the tag numbers from above, then swap roles and compare.
results_table: Leaves counted from bottom leaf to the leaf directly above it (n)
Fraction of a turn per leaf (t divided by n)
Angle per leaf in degrees (360 times t divided by n)

materials.item: a potted plant, garden plant or cut stem with at least 9 leaves growing one at a time up the stem, such as a hibiscus, chilli or brinjal plant (a neighbour's or school garden is fine)
a second plant or stem to compare, ideally of a different kind
12 small paper tags or sticky notes, numbered 0 to 11, for each stem. If they fall off in damp weather, tie paper tags loosely to the leaf stalks with thread
a length of thread, about 1 metre
a pencil and a notebook for the table
a calculator or scrap paper for the angles

experiments.safety: Do not pick leaves or bend the stem. Use only plants you know are safe to touch. Some plants, such as chilli, can sting the eyes, and brinjal stems can have small thorns, so keep hands away from your face and touch gently. Wash hands afterwards. Do not taste any leaf.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for each stem. Draw the stem seen from above, with the leaves in order and an arrow showing which way they turn.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you tag the leaves of a real stem, follow a thread round it and work out how far each leaf turns from the last. You compare your result with the fractions that plants often use.

setup.art: A potted plant with small numbered paper tags on the leaves from 0 at the bottom up to 8 near the top.
setup.caption: 1. Tag the leaves from the bottom up: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on.

setup.art: The same plant seen from above with the leaves drawn in a spiral and a thread joining leaf 0, leaf 1, leaf 2 round the stem.
setup.caption: 2. Find the first leaf directly above leaf 0. Follow the leaves in order with a thread.

setup.art: A table with columns for leaves, turns, fraction and angle, with the row for the first plant filled in as 5 leaves, 2 turns, 2 over 5 and 144 degrees.
setup.caption: 3. Count the leaves and the turns. Work out the fraction and the angle.

flow.do: Show your child the plant. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: The leaves climb the stem. Does each leaf turn half a circle from the last, or less? How many leaves before one sits directly above the first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves on the stem. How far does each leaf turn? Why do you think so?

ask.q: How far do you think each leaf turns round the stem from the last one?
good: Half a circle, so the leaves are on two sides.
A little less than half.
It is random.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Staircase. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Stick tag 0 on a leaf near the bottom of the stem. Move up the stem. Stick tag 1 on the next leaf up, tag 2 on the one after, and so on. Always go to the next leaf up, not the one beside it.
flow.say: Tag the lowest leaf 0. Now go up the stem. The next leaf up is 1. Then 2. Do not skip any leaf. Each tag goes on the very next leaf up.
flow.kid: Tag the bottom leaf 0. Tag the next leaf up 1. Keep going up.
flow.parent: Stems lean a little, so look from the top to see which leaf is next. If two leaves come out at the same height, tag them in turn. This plan works best for plants with leaves one at a time. Plants with leaves in pairs, such as tulsi or mint, are a good extra test.
flow.context: In this step, you tag the leaves in order up the stem.

flow.do: Look down on the plant. Find the first leaf directly above leaf 0, on the same side of the stem. Note its number, n. Tie the thread loosely to leaf 0. Take it to leaf 1, then 2, and on up to leaf n, always the short way round the stem. Count how many times the thread goes round the stem. Call this t.
flow.say: Look from above. Which is the first leaf directly above leaf 0? That is n. Now wind the thread round the stem from leaf to leaf. How many times did it go round?
flow.kid: Find the first leaf above leaf 0 on the same side. Follow the thread round. Count the turns.
flow.parent: Do not worry if no leaf is exactly above. Choose the closest, within about a quarter of a turn either side. Typical results are n and t of 2 and 1, 3 and 1, 5 and 2, or 8 and 3. If the thread goes round the stem a different number of times when you check, use the second count.

check.q: A thread winds twice round the stem from leaf 0 to the first leaf directly above it, which is leaf 5. How many degrees does each leaf turn from the last?
check.why: Two turns over five leaves is 2 over 5 of a turn for each leaf. 360 times 2, divided by 5, is 144 degrees. 72 degrees would be 1 over 5 of a turn, and 180 degrees would be half a turn.

flow.context: In this step, you find the leaf directly above the first and count the turns of the thread.

flow.do: Work out t divided by n, the fraction of a turn per leaf. Multiply by 360 to find the angle. Write both in the table. Compare your fraction with 1 over 2, 1 over 3, 2 over 5 and 3 over 8.
flow.say: Divide the turns by the leaves. That is how much of a circle each leaf turns. Multiply by 360 for the angle. Is it close to one of the fractions on the board?
flow.kid: Divide turns by leaves. Multiply by 360 for the angle.

ask.q: Which of 1 over 2, 1 over 3, 2 over 5 and 3 over 8 is your fraction nearest to?
good: 2 over 5.
3 over 8.
1 over 2.

flow.parent: The fractions are 180, 120, 144 and 135 degrees. Many plants are near 2 over 5 or 3 over 8. Both are close to the golden angle, 137.5 degrees. Do not worry if your stem is not tidy. Real stems are never perfect.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the fraction and the angle per leaf.

flow.do: Do the same for a second plant or a second stem. Fill in the next row of the table.
flow.say: Now try a different plant. Is it the same fraction, or a different one?
flow.kid: Try a second plant. Is it the same?

ask.q: Did the second plant have the same fraction as the first?
good: No, it was different.
Yes, both were about the same.
It was close but not the same.

flow.parent: Different plants often differ. A plant with leaves in pairs gives a pattern of pairs, with each pair turned a quarter of a circle from the last. This is a different arrangement from the one-at-a-time leaves.
flow.context: In this step, you test a second plant and compare.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found. Write the claim, the evidence and the reason.
flow.say: What did you find? What numbers show it? Why might a plant turn the leaves by this much and not by half a circle?
flow.kid: What did you find? Which numbers show it? Why not half a circle?

ask.q: Why might it help a plant to turn each leaf by about 140 degrees and not by half a circle?
good: With half a circle, leaves would line up in two rows and shade each other.
A turn like 140 degrees spreads the leaves so each gets light.

flow.parent: A strong answer says: a half turn puts leaf 2 straight over leaf 0, so the leaves line up and shade each other. A turn near 137.5 degrees never lines a leaf up exactly above an earlier leaf, so leaves spread out and share the light.

check.q: Which turn between neighbouring leaves would line up every second leaf above the one before it?
check.why: Half a circle twice is a whole circle, so leaf 2 sits directly above leaf 0. The golden angle never lines leaves up exactly, which is better for sharing light.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and why the turn matters to the plant.

activities.title: Grow a Koch Curve: a 27 centimetre line that keeps getting longer

materials.item: a sheet of plain A4 paper, turned sideways
a ruler and a sharp pencil
a compass from the geometry box (best), or a set square with a 60 degree corner, or a protractor
an eraser
a coloured pencil or pen
a calculator, or scrap paper for the lengths

activities.safety: The compass point is sharp: keep it down on the paper and let a grown-up help younger children. Sharpen pencils with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Draw a 27 centimetre line, replace its middle third with a tent, do it again on every piece, and measure the length each time.

activities.record: A table with columns for the round, the number of pieces, the length of each piece and the total length. Add your guess for round 3.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a Koch curve by repeating one rule on a straight line, and you measure how its length grows. You find the pattern in the lengths.

setup.art: A straight line 27 centimetres long on a sheet of paper with dots marking the thirds at 9 and 18 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line 27 centimetres long. Mark the thirds at 9 and 18 centimetres.

setup.art: The same line with the middle third rubbed out and a tent of two 9 centimetre sides drawn in its place.
setup.caption: 2. Rub out the middle third. Draw a tent with two sides of 9 centimetres.

setup.art: The curve with four pieces, each with a smaller tent of two 3 centimetre sides drawn on its middle third.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same on each of the four pieces, with tents of 3 centimetres.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a straight line 27 centimetres long, near the middle of the page. Ask them to guess what happens to the length if you replace the middle third with a tent.
flow.say: Here is a line 27 centimetres long. We will cut out the middle third and put in a tent. Will the new line be longer, shorter or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a line 27 centimetres long. Will a tent in the middle make it longer or shorter?

ask.q: Will the line with a tent be longer, shorter or the same length? Why?
good: Longer, because the tent goes up and down.
The same, because we only moved it.
Longer, because there are two sides in place of one.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Most children say the same or longer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Grow a Koch Curve. You guess before you draw.

flow.do: Mark dots at 9 and 18 centimetres on the line. Rub out the line between the dots. At the left dot, draw a line of 9 centimetres going up and to the right at 60 degrees. At the right dot, draw a line of 9 centimetres going up and to the left at 60 degrees. They meet at a point. (With a compass set to 9 centimetres, put the point on each dot in turn and draw two small arcs that cross: the crossing is the top of the tent.) Add the lengths: 9, 9, 9 and 9.
flow.say: Mark the thirds. Rub out the middle piece. Draw the two sides of a tent, each 9 centimetres long. They meet at the top. Now add up the four pieces.
flow.kid: Mark the thirds. Rub out the middle. Draw a tent with two 9 centimetre sides.
flow.parent: The tent sides and the rubbed-out piece are each 9 centimetres, so they make an equilateral triangle with the missing base. A 60 degree set square or a compass makes this easy. The total is 9 plus 9 plus 9 plus 9, which is 36 centimetres.

check.q: After one round, the Koch curve has 4 pieces, each 9 centimetres long. What is the total length?
check.why: 4 pieces of 9 centimetres is 4 times 9, which is 36 centimetres. The line got longer because 2 sides of the tent replaced the 1 piece that was rubbed out.

flow.context: In this step, you do round 1 and measure the new length.

flow.do: Look at each of the four pieces. For each one, find the middle third, which is 3 centimetres. Rub it out and draw a tent with two sides of 3 centimetres. Always put the tent on your left as you walk along the piece from the left end of the page. Count the pieces and add the lengths.
flow.say: Do the same to every piece. Find its middle third. That is 3 centimetres. Rub it out and put in a small tent. Keep the tent on your left as you walk along the curve.
flow.kid: Do the same on each of the four pieces. Use 3 centimetre tents.
flow.parent: There will be 16 pieces of 3 centimetres, so the length is 48 centimetres. The tents on the slanting pieces point to the left of the walking direction. Do not worry if the tents are not perfect. The shape is still a Koch curve. The compass method (set to 3 centimetres) works on slanting pieces, where a set square is awkward. With 2 to 4 children, each takes one of the four pieces for round 2 on a shared drawing, then everyone checks one another's tents and adds up the total together. One child alone, with a parent, does all four pieces.
flow.context: In this step, you do round 2 and measure the new length.

flow.do: Fill in the table for rounds 0, 1 and 2. Ask your child to find the pattern in the lengths and to guess rounds 3 and 4. Then test round 3 on one 3 centimetre piece.
flow.say: The lengths are 27, 36 and 48. How many times bigger does the length get each round? Can you guess the next two lengths?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Find the pattern. Guess the next two lengths.

ask.q: What is the pattern in the lengths, and what comes next?
good: 36 is 27 times 4 over 3. 48 is 36 times 4 over 3.
Each time it is one third longer. Next is 64.
It goes up by 9, then 12, then 16.

flow.parent: Round 3 has 64 pieces of 1 centimetre, so 64 centimetres. Round 4 has 256 pieces of one third of a centimetre, so about 85 centimetres. To check the guess for round 3 without drawing 64 tiny pieces, draw round 3 on just one 3 centimetre piece: it becomes 4 pieces of 1 centimetre, so 4 centimetres, one third longer. Each round multiplies the length by 4 over 3, which is the same as adding one third.

check.q: Each round of a Koch curve makes the line 4 over 3 times as long. The length is 48 centimetres after round 2. What is it after round 3?
check.why: One third of 48 is 16, and 48 plus 16 is 64. Multiplying 48 by 4 over 3 gives the same answer. Doubling to 96 would be too much, and adding 4 would be too little.

flow.context: In this step, you find the pattern in the lengths.

flow.do: Ask your child to imagine going on for ever. Show them that three Koch curves joined in a triangle make a snowflake. Ask the question below.
flow.say: If we kept going for ever, how long would the line be? Could it ever fit on the page? Does it ever stop?
flow.kid: Keep going for ever. How long would the line be? Would it fit on the page?

ask.q: If the rule were repeated for ever, would the line fit on the page, and how long would it be?
good: It would fit on the page but be endless in length.
It would never stop getting longer.
It would be longer than any number.

flow.parent: The curve never leaves the page, because the tents stay small. Yet the length grows by one third each round, without end. This is why the curve is a fractal.
flow.context: In this step, you think about the curve going on for ever.

activities.title: Equal Gaps or Growing Gaps? A rope coil against a shell

materials.item: a coil of thick rope or jute string that you lay flat in a spiral on the floor, a coir mat, a murukku that has been made already, or a picture of a coil
an empty shell of a garden snail (common in gardens after rain), a shankha or a shell from a shell stall, or a picture of a pointed shell or a nautilus. Two different shells are better than one
a school ruler with millimetres
a pencil and a notebook
a calculator, or scrap paper for dividing

activities.safety: Use only empty shells, and wash them and your hands afterwards. Never take a living snail. If you use a murukku, it is food: check for allergies such as sesame, and do not eat the one you measured. Broken shells can have sharp edges, so handle them with care.

schedule.what: Measure the gaps between the turns of a rope coil and a shell. Find out whether the gaps are equal or growing, and by how much.

activities.record: A table with the width of each turn for the coil and for the shell, and the ratio of each turn to the one before.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure the turns of a coil and of a shell, and find out which grows by adding the same amount and which by multiplying by the same fraction.

setup.art: A coil of rope seen from above with a ruler laid across its middle and the widths of three turns marked by arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the ruler across the middle of the coil. Mark where each turn crosses the ruler.

setup.art: A pointed shell lying on its side with a ruler beside it, and the width of the last three whorls marked by arrows.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the width of each whorl of the shell, from the biggest to the smallest.

setup.art: A table with columns for the whorl number, its width, and the width divided by the width of the next smaller whorl.
setup.caption: 3. Divide each width by the one before it.

flow.do: Show your child the coil and the shell. Ask them to guess whether the gaps will be equal or growing. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Look at the coil and the shell. Are the turns the same distance apart all the way out, or do they get further apart? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the coil and the shell. Are the gaps equal, or do they grow?

ask.q: Do you think the gaps in each will be equal or growing? Why?
good: The rope will be equal and the shell will grow.
Both will be equal.
Both will grow.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of Equal Gaps or Growing Gaps. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Lay the ruler across the middle of the coil. Starting at the centre, measure the distance from each turn to the next. Write the gaps. Do the same on a second line across a different part of the coil.
flow.say: Lay the ruler across the middle. Measure from one turn to the next, going outwards. Write each gap. Are they the same?
flow.kid: Lay the ruler across the coil. Measure each gap. Are the gaps the same?
flow.parent: A rope coil has gaps that are almost the same, within a millimetre or two. A murukku made with a press is also nearly equal. If your gaps differ by more than a few millimetres, check that the ruler goes through the centre.

check.q: A coil has gaps of 12, 12 and 11 millimetres. Which kind of spiral grows by adding the same amount each turn?
options: An Archimedean spiral, like this coil
A logarithmic spiral, like a shell
check.why: When the gaps are about equal, the coil grows by adding the same amount each turn. That is an Archimedean spiral. A shell has growing gaps.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the gaps in the coil.

flow.do: Measure the width of each whorl of the shell, from the biggest to the smallest. Hold the ruler across the shell at the same place each time. Write the widths in a list. If you have no shell, measure a picture of one.
flow.say: Hold the shell with the tip up. Measure the width of each whorl. Start with the biggest. Write them down.
flow.kid: Measure the width of each whorl, from the biggest to the smallest.
flow.parent: A pointed shell may have five or six whorls. Measure at the widest part of each. Hold the ruler at the same angle each time. The small whorls near the tip are hard to measure, so stop when the whorls are too small. If you have no shell, search for a photo of a pointed shell, hold the ruler to the screen and use the pictured widths.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the width of each whorl of a shell.

flow.do: Subtract each width from the one next to it. Then divide each width by the next smaller one. Write both answers. Ask which of the two is nearly the same each time.
flow.say: Take away each width from the one before it. Do the answers match? Now divide each width by the one before it. Which gives nearly the same answer each time?
flow.kid: Take away. Then divide. Which gives the same answer each time?

ask.q: Did taking away or dividing give nearly the same answer each time?
good: Dividing.
The take-aways kept getting bigger but the divisions stayed near the same.
Dividing gave about 1.5 each time.

flow.parent: For a shell, the take-aways grow while the divisions stay near the same number, often between 1.2 and 2. That number is the fraction by which each whorl is wider than the last. Some shells are less regular, especially if the shell is damaged or the growth was uneven. Real shells are only roughly regular: if the divisions are within about 0.2 of one another while the take-aways clearly grow, the shell passes.
