If nothing is steady, say so honestly; the shell may be damaged, or you may have measured at different places. With 2 to 4 children, each measures a different shell, then compare the ratios. Two shells of the same kind should give similar ratios, and different kinds can differ. One child alone measures two shells with a parent.

check.q: A shell has whorl widths of 10, 15 and 22.5 millimetres. What do you get by dividing each width by the one before?
options: About 1.5 each time, so the shell grows by a fraction
5 and 7.5, so the shell grows by adding
check.why: 15 divided by 10 is 1.5, and 22.5 divided by 15 is 1.5. The ratio is the same each time, which is what a shell does. The take-aways are 5 and 7.5, which are not the same.

flow.context: In this step, you take away and divide the widths to see which rule the shell follows.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain the difference between the two spirals.
flow.say: What is the difference between the way the rope coils and the way the shell coils? Which one keeps the same shape as it grows?
flow.kid: How is the shell different from the rope? Which keeps its shape?

ask.q: How does the shell grow differently from the rope coil?
good: The shell grows by multiplying, and the rope by adding.
The shell's gaps get bigger. The rope's stay the same.
The shell keeps the same shape as it gets bigger.

flow.context: In this step, you say how the shell and the rope differ.

activities.title: Fold a Dragon: a fractal from a paper strip

materials.item: 4 thin strips of paper, each about 1.5 centimetres wide and about 55 centimetres long, made by cutting plain A4 sheets lengthwise and joining two with tape (a wider strip is too bulky and the folded dragon will overlap itself)
clear tape
a ruler
a pencil
a coloured pen

activities.safety: A grown-up helps younger children with the scissors when cutting the paper strips. Fold slowly: thin paper can give a paper cut.

schedule.what: Fold a strip in half 1, 2, 3 and 4 times, open each fold to a right angle, and draw the shapes.

activities.record: Draw the shape you get after 1, 2, 3 and 4 folds. Write the number of creases for each.
activities.context: In this activity, you fold a paper strip in half again and again in the same direction, then open it up and see a curve that gets more complicated with every fold.

setup.art: A long paper strip folded in half once, then twice, with the right end brought over to the left end each time.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the strip in half. Fold it in half again in the same direction.

setup.art: The strip opened so every crease is a right angle, forming a zig-zag with three corners.
setup.caption: 2. Open the strip and set each crease to a right angle.

setup.art: Four opened strips in a row, with 1, 3, 7 and 15 corners, each outlined with a coloured pen.
setup.caption: 3. Fold 3 and 4 times. Draw each shape.

flow.do: Show the strip. Ask your child to guess what shape appears. You will fold the strip in half, then in half again. Then you will open it with the folds at right angles.
flow.say: We will fold a strip in half, and in half again, always the same way. Then we will open it with every fold at a right angle. What shape do you think we will get? Why?
flow.kid: Fold the strip twice. Open the folds to right angles. What shape will you see?

ask.q: What shape do you think the folded strip will make?
good: A zig-zag.
A square.
A staircase.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fold a Dragon. You guess before you fold.

flow.do: Take one strip. Fold the right end to the left end, to make a half-length strip. Open it and look at the one crease. Then fold in half again the same way and open it. There are now three creases. Open each crease to a right angle. Lay the strip on paper and trace it.
flow.say: Fold the right end to the left end. Always the same direction. Fold again. Open it out. Each crease becomes a right angle. Trace the shape.
flow.kid: Fold the strip in half twice, the same way. Open it. Make each fold a right angle.
flow.parent: The folds must always go the same way: right end over to the left end. If you flip the strip over between folds, you will get a different shape. Open the creases so the strip makes right angles and stands flat on the page.

check.q: A strip is folded in half twice and opened. How many creases does it have?
check.why: The first fold makes 1 crease. The second fold makes a crease in each of the two halves, and the first crease stays. That is 1 plus 2, which is 3 creases.

flow.context: In this step, you fold the strip twice and trace the shape.

flow.do: Take a new strip and fold it in half three times in the same direction. Open it and set the creases to right angles. Trace the shape. Do the same with a fourth strip folded four times. Count the creases each time.
flow.say: Fold again, one more time each. Three folds, then four folds. Always the same way. Open and trace. Count the creases.
flow.kid: Fold three times. Open. Trace. Then fold four times. Open. Trace.
flow.parent: After three folds there are 7 creases, and after four there are 15. After four folds, the shape starts to look like a curly dragon with curls. After five folds the paper is thick and hard to fold, so stop at four. If the creases will not hold, press each one flat with a ruler edge. With 2 to 4 children, each folds and traces their own strip, then lay the shapes side by side to compare. One child alone, with a parent, can fold one strip each and compare.
flow.context: In this step, you fold 3 and 4 times and trace each shape.

flow.do: Fill in the number of creases for 1, 2, 3 and 4 folds. Ask your child to find the pattern and to guess the creases after 5 folds.
flow.say: The creases are 1, 3, 7 and 15. What do you notice? How many creases after five folds?
flow.kid: The creases are 1, 3, 7 and 15. What is the pattern?

ask.q: What is the pattern in the number of creases, and what is next?
good: Double and add 1. After 15 comes 31.
Each is one less than a power of 2.

flow.parent: Each fold doubles the creases and adds one more. So 1 becomes 3, 3 becomes 7, 7 becomes 15 and 15 becomes 31. The number is always one less than 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32.

check.q: A strip folded 4 times has 15 creases. How many creases would it have after 5 folds?
check.why: Each fold doubles the creases and adds one. 15 doubled is 30, plus 1 is 31. The answer 30 forgets the extra crease. The answer 16 only adds one.

flow.context: In this step, you find the pattern in the creases.

flow.do: Compare the shapes after 3 and 4 folds. Ask your child how the bigger shape contains the smaller shape.
flow.say: Look at the shape after four folds. Can you see the shape from three folds inside it? What does that remind you of?
flow.kid: Look at the four-fold shape. Can you see the three-fold shape inside?

ask.q: Can you find a smaller dragon inside the bigger one?
good: Yes, the first half is the same shape as the earlier dragon.
Each part looks like a smaller dragon.
It looks like the Koch curve, with a shape made of smaller copies.

flow.parent: The curve after many folds is called the dragon curve. It was first worked out by three physicists, John Heighway, Bruce Banks and William Harter, in 1966, and it was made famous by the writer Martin Gardner in 1967. Each part looks like a smaller dragon, so it is a fractal. If you folded for ever, the dragon curve would cover a patch of the page without crossing itself.
flow.context: In this step, you compare the shapes after different numbers of folds.

activities.title: The Chaos Game: a pattern from dots chosen by a die

materials.item: a sheet of plain A4 paper, turned sideways
a ruler with millimetres
a sharp pencil
a die
a coloured pen for the corners

activities.safety: Sharpen pencils with a grown-up, or use a sharpener with a cover.

schedule.what: Mark three corners, roll a die and move halfway to a corner again and again. See what pattern the dots make.

activities.record: Stick your page in your notebook. Write how many dots you made, and what shape they made.
activities.context: In this activity, you place dots using a die and one simple rule. You see whether chance can build an exact pattern.

setup.art: A sheet with three corners marked A at the bottom left, B at the bottom right and C at the top middle, about 18 centimetres apart.
setup.caption: 1. Mark three corners, A, B and C, about 18 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A pencil dot, a die showing 4 beside it and a ruler measuring halfway from the dot to the corner B.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. 1 or 2 means A, 3 or 4 means B, 5 or 6 means C. Measure halfway to that corner.

setup.art: The triangle after about 50 dots, with an empty hole in the middle and a pattern of smaller empty triangles around it.
setup.caption: 3. Make a new dot there. Repeat 50 times. See what shape appears.

flow.do: On the page, mark corner A at the bottom left and corner B at the bottom right. Mark corner C at the top middle. Each corner is about 18 centimetres from the others. Write the letters. Ask your child to guess what the dots will look like after 50 rolls.
flow.say: Three corners, and a die to choose. The rule is to move halfway to the corner the die picks, and put a dot. What will the dots look like after fifty rolls? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mark three corners. Guess what the dots will look like after 50 rolls.

ask.q: What shape do you think the dots will make?
good: A triangle full of dots.
A mess.
A pattern with holes.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect a filled triangle or a mess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Chaos Game. You guess before you play.

flow.do: Put a first dot anywhere inside the triangle. Write a small 0 beside it.
flow.say: Put a first dot anywhere inside the triangle. This dot is where we start.
flow.kid: Put a dot anywhere inside the triangle.
flow.context: In this step, you put the starting dot.

flow.do: Roll the die. If it shows 1 or 2, go towards A. If 3 or 4, go towards B. If 5 or 6, go towards C. Measure the distance from your last dot to that corner. Put a new dot halfway. Repeat until you have 50 dots.
flow.say: Roll. Choose the corner. Measure to it. Put the dot at the halfway point. Then roll again from that dot. Keep going for fifty dots.
flow.kid: Roll. Pick a corner. Put a dot halfway to it. Do this 50 times.
flow.parent: Measuring in millimetres helps. A ruler placed from the dot to the corner gives the distance, and half of it is the new place. Ignore the first three or four dots. They may fall outside the pattern. Fifty dots take about 12 to 15 minutes alone. If it is slow, stop at 40 dots, or share the work: one person rolls and calls the corner, one measures, and one marks the dot. Swap jobs every 10 dots. Do not worry about small errors; each halving shrinks an earlier mistake. No die: pick a paper chit from a bowl of six chits marked A, A, B, B, C, C, and put it back each time. Two to four children can each make their own page and then compare how the holes fall, which shows that chance changes the dots but not the pattern.
flow.context: In this step, you place the dots using the die.

flow.do: Look at the dots together. Ask where there are gaps, and what shape the gaps make.
flow.say: Look at the page. Are there places with no dots? What shape are they? What do you see inside the gaps?
flow.kid: Look at the dots. Where are there gaps? What shape are the gaps?

ask.q: What do you notice about the gaps in the dots?
good: There is a hole in the middle, shaped like a triangle.
There are smaller holes round the edges too.
The dots make triangles with triangles inside.

flow.parent: After 50 dots, the middle of the triangle usually has a clear hole, and smaller holes appear nearer the corners. With 50 dots the holes are only hinted at: it is typical, not exact, so say what you see. With 200 or more dots, the pattern becomes the Sierpinski triangle, a triangle made of three smaller triangles, each made of three smaller ones, and so on. It is a triangle with triangles inside triangles.

check.q: In the Chaos Game, the dots go wherever the die says. Why does the same pattern still appear each time?
options: The rule of moving halfway to a corner never lands a dot in the middle holes, however the die falls
The die is not really random
check.why: Each move goes halfway to a corner, so after the first few dots every dot lands on the pattern and the big holes are never reached, however the die falls. The die chooses the order, and the rule decides the shape.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the pattern the dots make.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what surprised them. Ask them to think of one more thing where a simple rule and chance make a pattern.
flow.say: Chance chose each corner, but the shape came out the same way each time. What surprised you? Where else might a simple rule and chance make a pattern?
flow.kid: Chance chose each corner. The shape still appeared. What surprised you?

ask.q: Where else might a simple rule and chance make a pattern?
good: Snow falling in a pile.
The branching cluster in the Stick and Wander game.
Raindrops on a window.

flow.context: In this step, you say what surprised you and think of another example.

projects.title: A Sierpinski Wall Hanging: 27 triangles in three days

materials.item: coloured paper or thin card, in two colours (old gift wrap or magazine pages work too), 2 to 4 sheets of A4 in all
a ruler and a pencil
scissors, used by a grown-up or with a grown-up beside the child
a glue stick
a backing sheet of card about 40 centimetres across
a card triangle template with sides of 4 centimetres (made from a cereal box or a spare piece of card)

projects.safety: Younger children cut with a grown-up beside them. Cut away from the fingers.

schedule.what: Make a 4 centimetre triangle template and cut out 27 triangles.
Glue the triangles into 9 groups of 3, so each group is a triangle with a hole.
Glue the 9 groups into 3 bigger groups, and then into one big triangle on the backing card.

projects.record: A table showing the level, how many triangles are in each shape, and what fraction of the big triangle is covered with paper.
projects.context: In this project, you build a Sierpinski triangle out of paper triangles over three days. You see how a simple rule repeated makes a shape with holes inside holes.

setup.art: Twenty-seven small coloured paper triangles in rows on a table next to a card template, a ruler and scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out 27 small triangles using the template.

setup.art: Three small triangles glued corner to corner into a bigger triangle with an empty triangular hole in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Glue 3 triangles corner to corner. This makes a triangle with a hole.

setup.art: Three of those bigger triangles glued corner to corner, and then three of those, making a large triangle with holes inside holes.
setup.caption: 3. Glue 3 of these together, and then 3 of those, until you have one big triangle.

flow.do: On day 1, draw a triangle with three sides of 4 centimetres on card and cut it out as a template. Trace it on the coloured paper 27 times. A grown-up cuts them out. Count the pieces.
flow.say: Make a template triangle with every side 4 centimetres. Trace it on the coloured paper. We need 27 of them. Count as you go.
flow.kid: Make a template. Trace 27 triangles. Cut them out.
flow.parent: To draw a triangle with three equal sides, use a set square or a protractor, or measure a 4 centimetre line and use a thread of 4 centimetres to find the third point. Alternate two colours if you like. Stack several sheets so one cut makes several triangles.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Sierpinski wall hanging. You cut out the triangles.

flow.do: On day 2, glue the triangles in groups of 3. Put two triangles side by side with the corners touching, then the third on top, touching both. Make 9 groups. Count the holes. Triangles that touch only at corners hold badly. Overlap each corner by 5 millimetres and glue the overlap.
flow.say: Today we make groups of three. Two triangles sit at the bottom, touching at the corners. The third sits on top. There is a triangular hole in the middle. Make nine groups.
flow.kid: Glue 3 triangles into one group. Make 9 groups.

check.q: A group of 3 small triangles is glued corner to corner into a bigger triangle. What is in the middle of the bigger triangle?
check.why: Three triangles meeting corner to corner leave an empty triangle in the middle, upside down. That hole is the first hole in the Sierpinski pattern.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Sierpinski wall hanging. You glue 9 groups of 3 triangles.

flow.do: On day 3, lightly draw a guide triangle with 32 centimetre sides on the backing card. Lay 3 of the groups corner to corner to make a bigger group. Make 3 of these. Lay the 3 big groups corner to corner inside the guide. Check the holes, then glue every group down onto the card, in its place. Count the holes of different sizes.
flow.say: Now we put 3 groups together, then 3 of those, on the card. The same rule, bigger each time. How many sizes of hole can you see?
flow.kid: Lay 3 groups together. Make 3 bigger groups. Place them in one big triangle, then glue them down on the card.

ask.q: How many different sizes of triangular hole do you see?
good: Three sizes: small, medium and big.
A big one in the middle and smaller ones in the groups.

flow.parent: The finished triangle has 27 paper triangles and holes of three sizes. The paper covers 27 out of 64 of the area of a full triangle of the same side, which is a little less than half. If you carried on for ever, the paper would cover less and less, and in the end almost nothing. One child with a parent spreads the work over three days. Three children can finish in one sitting: each cuts 9 triangles, makes 3 groups and builds one big group of 9, then the three big groups go on the card together. Four children: the fourth draws the guide triangle and checks the holes. Scissors and glue are the only things to watch; a glue stick is safe for children.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Sierpinski wall hanging. You build the big triangle.

challenges.title: Water for Every Pot: one pipe to sixteen plants
challenges.problem: A terrace has 16 plant pots in a 4 by 4 square, each pot 30 centimetres from its neighbours. A tap sits in the middle of the square. Draw a pipe network on squared paper so that water has to travel the same distance to every pot, using as little pipe as you can.
constraints: Draw on squared paper, with 1 square standing for 15 centimetres. The pots sit on the grid points, 2 squares apart.
Pipes must run along the grid lines.
The tap is in the middle of the 4 by 4 square of pots.
The distance from the tap to every pot, along the pipes, must be exactly the same.
materials: a coloured pencil for the pipes
a calculator, or scrap paper for adding lengths
general: A star: a separate pipe from the tap to each pot, along the grid lines. This is easy, but the distances differ from pot to pot, and there is a lot of pipe.
A comb: one long pipe through the middle with side pipes to each pot. The distances differ from pot to pot.
creative: An H-tree: split the pipe into two, then each into two, again and again, so every pot is reached after the same number of splits. This is a fractal.
Try the same idea with 64 pots in an 8 by 8 square. How much more pipe do you need?
A tree that splits into three at each step. Does it still deliver water to every pot equally?
challenges.your_turn: Design your own network for the 16 pots. Work out the distance from the tap to each pot, and the total length of pipe. Then see whether a friend can find a network with less pipe that still gives equal distances.

setup.art: A squared page with 16 dots in a 4 by 4 square and a tap marked in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Mark 16 pots and the tap on squared paper.

setup.art: A star of straight pipes from the tap to 16 pots, with lengths of different sizes marked on each pipe.
setup.caption: 2. Try a star. Measure the distance to each pot.

setup.art: An H-shaped pipe network from the tap that splits into two, then into four, then into eight and sixteen, ending at the 16 pots.
setup.caption: 3. Try an H-tree. Add the lengths of all the pipes.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Mark the 16 pots and the tap on squared paper. Ask your child to sketch a first idea.
flow.say: Sixteen pots, and one tap in the middle. The water should reach every pot after the same distance. How could the pipes go? Draw a first idea.
flow.kid: Mark the 16 pots and the tap. Draw a first idea for the pipes.

ask.q: How could the pipes go so that every pot is the same distance from the tap?
good: Split the pipe into two again and again.
A pipe straight to each pot.
The same number of bends to every pot.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Water for Every Pot challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Draw a separate pipe from the tap to each pot, along the grid lines. Count the squares from the tap to the nearest pot and to the furthest pot. Add up the pipe.
flow.say: Try a star first. Is the nearest pot the same distance as the furthest? How much pipe is that in all?
flow.kid: Draw a pipe from the tap to every pot. Which pot is nearest? Which is furthest?
flow.parent: The star gives different distances for pots near to and far from the tap, so the near pots would get water first. This shows the problem to solve. Along the grid lines the nearest pots are 2 squares away and the furthest 6, and the separate pipes add up to 64 squares. Work alone with a parent, or in a group of 2 to 4 where each child designs a network and then everyone checks the others.
flow.context: In this step, you try a star-shaped network and find its weakness.

flow.do: Now draw an H-tree. From the tap, draw a pipe 2 squares left and 2 squares right. From each end, draw a pipe 2 squares up and 2 squares down. From each of those ends, draw a pipe 1 square left and 1 square right. From each of those ends, draw a pipe 1 square up and 1 square down. Check that each pipe ends at a pot. Add up the lengths from the tap to one pot, and to another.
flow.say: Draw the H in four steps. First two squares left and right. Then two squares up and down. Then one square left and right. Then one up and down. Every pot is reached. Is the distance the same for every pot?
flow.kid: Draw an H-tree step by step. Check it reaches every pot.

check.q: In the H-tree, the path to a pot is 2, then 2, then 1, then 1 squares. How many squares is the path to each pot, and is it the same for every pot?
options: 6 squares, and it is the same for every pot
6 squares for some pots and fewer for others
check.why: 2 plus 2 plus 1 plus 1 is 6 squares. Every pot is reached by the same four pieces in the same order, so every path is 6 squares. At 15 centimetres a square, that is 90 centimetres.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the H-tree and check the distances.

flow.do: Add up all the pipe in the H-tree. Count the pieces of each length. There are 2 pieces of 2 squares and 4 more of 2 squares. There are 8 of 1 square and 16 of 1 square. Compare it with the star.
flow.say: Add up all the pipe. How many pieces of each length? How much pipe in all? Which design uses less pipe, the star or the H?
flow.kid: Add up all the pipe in the H-tree. Compare it with the star.

ask.q: Which design is better, the star or the H-tree, and why?
good: The H-tree, because every pot gets water at the same time.
The star has pots at different distances, and it uses more pipe than the H-tree.
It depends on what you want.

flow.parent: The H-tree uses 36 squares of pipe, which is 36 times 15 centimetres, which is 540 centimetres. Every pot is 6 squares away. A star has pots at different distances and, along the grid lines, uses 64 squares of pipe, almost twice as much. If a child finds a network with less pipe and equal distances, check it carefully and celebrate.
flow.context: In this step, you add up the pipe and compare the designs.

items.p: A square is made twice as wide in every direction. Its area becomes how many times as big?
items.why: The new square can be cut into 4 copies of the old square, 2 along and 2 up. So its area is 4 times as big. A line would only grow 2 times.

items.p: A cube is made twice as long on every edge. Its volume becomes how many times as big?
items.why: The new cube holds 2 along, 2 across and 2 up, which is 2 times 2 times 2, or 8 copies of the old cube.

items.p: A straight line has dimension ____.
items.why: When you double a line, it grows 2 times, and 2 is 2 multiplied once. So its dimension is 1. A flat shape is 2 and a solid is 3.

items.p: When the boxes covering a straight line are cut to half their width, the line touches the same number of boxes.
items.why: False. Boxes half as wide need twice as many to cover the same line, so the count doubles. A filled page would need 4 times as many.

items.p: A coast's box count goes up by 3 times each time the boxes are halved. Which description fits?
opts: It is rougher than a straight line, and between a line and a page
items.why: A straight line gives 2 times and a filled page 4 times. A ratio of 3 is in between, so the coast is rougher than a line but does not fill the page.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Each turn a fixed fraction wider
Repeating one step on its own result
How size grows when a shape is doubled
A growing group of things stuck together
items.why: These five words are the vocabulary of this unit. A strong answer could give an example of each: a rope coil, a shell, folding a strip again and again, a line, and the shape from the Stick and Wander game.

items.p: Sort each spiral by how its coils grow.
items: a murukku made with a press
items.why: A coil that is pressed or laid down evenly has equal gaps. A shell grows by adding to the opening a bit wider each time, so its gaps grow.

items.p: Put the steps for making one round of a Koch curve in order.
items: Draw a tent whose two sides are as long as the piece you rubbed out
Rub out the middle third of the line
a: Rub out the middle third of the line
Draw a tent whose two sides are as long as the piece you rubbed out
items.why: First you need a line, then you mark the thirds so you know which piece to remove. Only after rubbing out the middle third can you put the tent in its place.

items.p: A Koch curve is 27 centimetres long. After one round it is 36 centimetres long. How long is it after two rounds?
items.why: Each round multiplies the length by 4 over 3, which is adding one third. One third of 36 is 12, and 36 plus 12 is 48.

items.p: A line made of 4 pieces, each 9 centimetres long, is ____ centimetres long in all.
items.why: 4 times 9 is 36. This is the length of a Koch curve after one round, starting from 27 centimetres.

items.p: Each whorl of a shell is 1.5 times as wide as the one before. The biggest whorl is 36 millimetres wide. How wide is the whorl just before it?
items.why: To go backwards, divide by 1.5. 36 divided by 1.5 is 24. The answer 54 goes the wrong way, and 18 divides by 2 instead of 1.5.

items.p: A small shell and a big shell of the same kind have the same shape, because each whorl is the same fraction wider than the last.
items.why: True. Growing by a fixed fraction keeps the shape the same. The big shell is the small shell scaled up.

items.p: A plant turns 2 over 5 of a circle between neighbouring leaves. How many degrees is that?
items.why: A full circle is 360 degrees. 360 times 2, divided by 5, is 144 degrees. 72 degrees is 1 over 5 of a circle.

items.p: In the leaf test, why would it be a poor plan for a plant to turn each leaf exactly half a circle from the last?
items.a: After two leaves the stem has made a whole turn, so the third leaf sits directly above the first. All the leaves line up in two rows. Each leaf shades the leaf below it, so the lower leaves get little light.
items.why: A strong answer says that half a turn twice is a whole turn, so leaves stack in two rows and shade each other.

items.p: Draw a Koch curve starting from a line 9 centimetres long. Draw the line, then round 1, and write the length after each.
items.a: A 9 centimetre line, then the same line with a tent of two 3 centimetre sides in the middle third. The lengths are 9 and 12 centimetres.
items.why: The middle third is 3 centimetres. Replacing it with two 3 centimetre sides adds 3 centimetres, so the length is 12. That is 9 times 4 over 3.

items.p: Label the drawing of a stem seen from above: write 0 on the lowest leaf, number the next four leaves in order, and draw an arrow to show which way the leaves turn.
items.a: The leaves numbered 0 to 4 in order round the stem, each a little further round, with a curved arrow in the direction they turn.
items.why: Leaves are numbered in the order they grow up the stem. In the view from above, the numbers go round the centre in one direction.
items.art: A plant stem seen from above with five unnumbered leaves arranged in a spiral round the middle.

items.p: A rough coastline has a roughness number of 1.5. What does that tell you?
opts: It is rougher than a coast with 1.3, and does not fill the page
It is exactly a straight line
items.why: The roughness number is between 1 for a straight line and 2 for a filled page. A larger number means a rougher edge that covers more of the page.

items.p: Which of these has a roughness number closest to 2?
opts: A line so crinkly that it nearly fills the page
A circle drawn with a compass
items.why: A roughness number near 2 means the line nearly fills the page. A straight line, a gentle curve and a circle all have a number near 1.

items.p: Each round of a Koch curve multiplies the length by 4 over ____.
items.why: Four pieces each a third as long as the old piece make 4 thirds of the old length. So each round multiplies the length by 4 over 3.

items.p: A Koch curve is 81 centimetres long. How long is it after three rounds?
items.why: Round 1: 81 times 4 over 3 is 108. Round 2: 108 times 4 over 3 is 144. Round 3: 144 times 4 over 3 is 192.

items.p: A Koch snowflake has an edge of endless length but an area that stays small.
items.why: True. Each round makes the edge longer, so it grows without end. But the tents are tiny and never leave the region around the triangle, so the area stays less than 1.6 times the starting triangle.

items.p: A teacher says a Koch curve is exactly self-similar but a real coast is self-similar only on average. What does that mean?
opts: No small part of a real coast is an exact copy of a bigger part, but the coast looks about as rough at every size
A Koch curve is not rough
Real coasts are exact copies of themselves
items.why: In a Koch curve each small piece is an exact copy of a bigger piece. A real coast only looks equally rough at different sizes, and only over a range of sizes.

items.p: A plant turns 3 over 8 of a circle between neighbouring leaves. After 8 leaves, how many whole turns has the stem made?
items.why: Each leaf turns 3 over 8 of a circle. Eight leaves turn 8 times 3 over 8, which is 3 whole circles.

items.p: A turn of 3 over 8 of a circle is ____ degrees.
items.why: 360 divided by 8 is 45, and 45 times 3 is 135. It is close to the golden angle of 137.5 degrees.

items.p: Match each turn to its angle.
items.why: Each angle is 360 degrees times the fraction. The fractions 2 over 5 and 3 over 8 land on either side of the golden angle.

items.p: Put these turns between neighbouring leaves in order, from the smallest angle to the biggest.
items.why: In degrees they are 120, 135, 137.5, 144 and 180. The fractions 3 over 8 and 2 over 5 are on either side of the golden angle.

items.p: Sort each spiral by what makes it.
cats: Moving air bent by the Earth's spin
Each coil a fixed fraction wider
Waves of squeezing in stars and gas
items: a cyclone over the Bay of Bengal
Moving air bent by the Earth's spin
Each coil a fixed fraction wider
Waves of squeezing in stars and gas
Each coil a fixed fraction wider
Moving air bent by the Earth's spin
items.why: The same spiral shape comes from three different causes. A shape does not tell you why it is there.

items.p: Walkers wander at random and stick to a growing cluster. Why do the tips grow fastest?
opts: A wandering walker meets a tip before it reaches a hollow
Walkers prefer to stick to arms
The die points towards the tips
items.why: A walker coming from outside meets the parts that stick out first. Those parts catch the most walkers and grow, while the hollows between arms stay hidden.

items.p: A rope coil and a shell are both spirals. Explain one way they are the same and one way they are different.
items.a: Both wind round a centre and get wider as they go out. The rope adds the same amount each turn, so its gaps are equal. The shell multiplies by a fixed fraction, so its gaps grow and its shape stays the same.
items.why: A strong answer names a similarity, such as winding round a centre, and the key difference between adding the same amount and multiplying by the same fraction.

items.p: A friend says a sink drains one way in India and the opposite way in Australia because of the Earth's spin. Is she right? Say what is true and what is not.
items.a: The Earth's spin does make cyclones spin in opposite directions in the northern and southern halves. But a sink is far too small for the effect to matter. The way a sink swirls depends on its shape and how the water was stirred.
items.why: A strong answer separates the cyclone, where the effect is real, from the sink, where it is too weak to notice.

items.p: Draw a tree where every branch splits into two shorter branches, with three levels of splitting. Count the tips.
items.a: A trunk that splits into 2, then 4, then 8 branches, so there are 8 tips.
items.why: Each level doubles the number of branches: 2, then 4, then 8. Doubling again and again grows the number of tips quickly.

items.p: Label the drawing of a stem seen from above: mark leaf 0, mark leaf 1, and write the angle between them if each leaf turns 2 over 5 of a circle.
items.a: Leaf 0 and leaf 1 marked, with an arc between them labelled 144 degrees.
items.why: 2 over 5 of 360 degrees is 144 degrees. A strong label shows the angle measured from leaf 0 to leaf 1 round the stem.
items.art: A stem seen from above with leaf 0 pointing to the top and a second leaf shown at a different angle.

items.p: Two friends discuss why plants often have Fibonacci numbers of spirals.

views.says: Plants use Fibonacci numbers because plants are good at maths.
Plants put each new leaf or seed where the gap is biggest. That simple rule happens to give the Fibonacci numbers.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend might have right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that the rule about gaps explains the numbers without the plant doing sums, which supports Meera. Aarav is right that the numbers are really there and that the plant's growth does something that behaves like maths. Scientists also still debate the exact process.
items.why: A strong answer prefers an explanation that uses a simple rule over one that uses an expert plant, and still gives the other friend credit. The exact process is still being studied.

items.p: A line's box counts are 6, 15 and 38 as the boxes are halved each time. What is the best estimate of its roughness number?
items.why: The ratios are 15 divided by 6, which is 2.5, and 38 divided by 15, which is about 2.5. A ratio of 2.5 gives a roughness number of about 1.3.

items.p: One line's box counts are 8, 16 and 32. Another's are 8, 32 and 128. What are their dimensions?
items.why: The first doubles each time, so its dimension is 1. The second quadruples each time, so its dimension is 2.

items.p: A real fern is an exact fractal because it repeats at every size.
items.why: False. A real fern repeats its leaflets for only three or four levels. Below that it is just smooth leaf tissue. Real things are only fractal over a range of sizes.

items.p: A paper strip folded in half 5 times in the same direction and then opened has ____ creases.
items.why: Each fold doubles the creases and adds one: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. After 5 folds there are 31.

items.p: A Koch curve starts 27 centimetres long. After how many rounds is it first longer than 1 metre?
items.why: The lengths are 36, 48, 64, 85 and about 114 centimetres after rounds 1 to 5. It first passes 100 centimetres at round 5.

items.p: The Koch snowflake has an edge of endless length and a small area. Explain why this is not a contradiction.
items.a: Each round adds many tiny tents, so the length grows without end. But the tents get smaller each time and stay close to the triangle, so the area they add shrinks quickly and never grows past a fixed limit.
items.why: A strong answer separates the edge, which grows by a fixed fraction each round and has no limit, from the area, which grows by smaller and smaller amounts.

items.p: Which is NOT a good reason for a plant to turn each leaf by about 137.5 degrees?
opts: It makes the leaves line up in straight rows
It stops one leaf from sitting exactly above another
It spreads the leaves round the stem
It gives every leaf a share of the light
items.why: A turn near 137.5 degrees never lines a leaf up exactly above another. That is why it spreads the leaves. Lining up in straight rows is what a half turn or a third turn does.

items.p: Two students talk about a measured coast.

views.says: A coast has one true roughness number, just as it has one true length in kilometres.
The number depends on the range of sizes you measure and how you do it, so a coast has no single true number.

items.ask: Which student do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other student has right.
items.a: A strong answer notes that a real coast is rough only over a range of sizes, and different ranges or methods give different numbers, which supports Dev. Neha is right that the numbers are often close and useful for comparing coasts. Scientists still debate how much weight the single number deserves.
items.why: A strong answer says what the number can do, which is compare coasts, and what it cannot do, which is claim to be the one truth about the coast.

items.p: Sort each shape by whether it is an exact fractal or a rough copy found in nature.
cats: Exact fractal (repeats for ever by a rule)
Rough copy (repeats only on average over some sizes)
items: a Koch curve drawn by a computer for ever
Exact fractal (repeats for ever by a rule)
Rough copy (repeats only on average over some sizes)
Rough copy (repeats only on average over some sizes)
a Sierpinski triangle made of endless smaller triangles
Exact fractal (repeats for ever by a rule)
Rough copy (repeats only on average over some sizes)
a tree seen from a window
Rough copy (repeats only on average over some sizes)
items.why: A mathematical fractal repeats for ever by a rule. Real coasts, ferns, cauliflowers and trees only look alike at a few sizes, and only roughly.

items.p: Match each cause to what it helps to make.
pairs: The Earth's spin bending moving air
Each coil a fixed fraction wider
items.why: Each shape has its own cause. The same words do not explain all of them, so a strong answer would add the evidence for each.

items.p: A computer model makes stripes like a zebra's. Does this prove that zebras make their stripes in the same way?
opts: No, a model that makes the right picture is not proof of the process
Only if the model is complicated
Only if the stripes are black and white
items.why: Many different processes can make the same picture. To show that the animal uses the process, scientists must find the chemicals or test what changes when they are altered.

items.p: A tree, a river delta and a lung all branch. Say what each one needs to reach or collect, and why branching helps.
items.a: A tree needs to reach light with many leaves and carry water to them. A river delta collects water from a wide area into one river. A lung needs to bring air close to blood over a very large surface. Branching lets one trunk reach or collect from every part of a space.
items.why: A strong answer names a job for each, and links branching to reaching every part of a space from one place.

items.p: Draw a spiral that grows by adding the same amount each turn, and a spiral that grows by multiplying by the same fraction. Label which is which.
items.a: A rope-like coil with equal gaps labelled adding, and a shell-like spiral with gaps growing wider labelled multiplying.
items.why: Equal gaps show growth by adding. Gaps that grow wider by the same fraction each turn show growth by multiplying, which keeps the shape.

items.p: Label the drawing of a shell with three whorl widths 24, 36 and 54 millimetres. Write the ratio between each neighbouring pair.
items.a: An arrow between 24 and 36 marked 1.5 and an arrow between 36 and 54 marked 1.5.
items.why: 36 divided by 24 is 1.5, and 54 divided by 36 is 1.5. The same ratio each time is the sign of a shell that keeps the same shape.
items.art: A pointed shell with three whorls marked with their widths, 24, 36 and 54 millimetres.

items.p: A plant turned each leaf by exactly 1 over 3 of a circle. What would happen to the leaves?
opts: They would line up in three straight rows and shade each other
They would spread evenly with no overlap
They would line up in one row
items.why: Three turns of a third make a whole circle, so every third leaf sits directly above another. The leaves stack in three rows and shade the ones below.

quiz.p: A square with sides 5 centimetres long is doubled to sides 10 centimetres long. How many of the small squares fit inside the big one?
quiz.why: The big square holds 2 small squares along and 2 up, which makes 4. So its area is 4 times as big. This is why a flat shape has dimension 2.

quiz.p: A straight line touches 6 boxes. The boxes are cut to half their width. How many boxes does the line touch?
quiz.why: A line has dimension 1, so halving the boxes doubles the count. 6 doubled is 12. 24 would be for a filled page.

quiz.p: A coast's box count rises from 10 to 24 when the boxes are halved. About what is the ratio?
quiz.why: 24 divided by 10 is 2.4. The ratio is between 2 for a line and 4 for a page, so the coast has a roughness number of about 1.3.

quiz.p: In a Koch curve, what do you do to every straight piece in each round?
opts: Replace its middle third with two sides of a tent
quiz.why: The rule is to cut out the middle third and put in the two sides of a tent. This makes every piece into four shorter pieces.

quiz.p: Why can a Koch curve have endless length and still fit on a page?
opts: Each round adds length, but the tents get smaller and stay on the page
quiz.why: Each round multiplies the length by 4 over 3, so there is no limit. But the new tents are tiny and stay near the old line, so the curve never leaves the page.

quiz.p: Which statement describes how a snail shell grows?
opts: Each whorl is a fixed fraction wider than the last
Each whorl is the same amount wider than the last
Each whorl is narrower than the last
Each whorl has a random width
quiz.why: A shell grows by multiplying by the same fraction, so the shape stays the same. Adding the same amount is how a rope coil grows.

quiz.p: Whorls of a broken shell measure 45 and 30 millimetres, widest first, and the ratio between whorls is the same all the way. What is the next smaller whorl?
quiz.why: 45 divided by 30 is 1.5. To go backwards, divide by 1.5, and 30 divided by 1.5 is 20. Subtracting 15 would be wrong, because a shell multiplies and does not add.

quiz.p: A plant turns 1 over 3 of a circle from one leaf to the next. How many degrees is that?
quiz.why: A full circle is 360 degrees, and 360 divided by 3 is 120 degrees.

quiz.p: Which turn between leaves is closest to the golden angle?
quiz.why: 3 over 8 of a circle is 135 degrees, which is the closest to the golden angle of about 137.5 degrees. 1 over 3 is 120 degrees, 1 over 4 is 90 and 1 over 2 is 180.

quiz.p: Which problem does the branching of the airways help a lung solve?
opts: Fitting a very large surface for air into a small space

quiz.p: A shell and a cyclone are both spirals. What does this tell you?
opts: The same shape can come from different causes
quiz.why: A shell grows by a fixed fraction. A cyclone spirals because of the Earth's spin. A shared shape does not mean a shared cause.

applications: Doctors and scientists use box counting and similar numbers to describe how branched a lung, a blood supply or a tumour is.
Map-makers state the scale at which a coast was measured, because the length depends on it.
Engineers build fractal antennas that fold a long wire into a small space so a phone can catch several wavelengths.
Computer artists use a few simple rules and a die to draw ferns, clouds and mountains for films and games.
Plant breeders and gardeners use the arrangement of leaves to space plants so that every leaf gets light.
Shell researchers use a few numbers to describe and compare the shapes of coiled shells, including fossils.
Weather forecasters track the spiral of a cyclone to predict where it will land and how strong it will be.
Chemists and physicists use random-walker models to understand how crystals, soot and metals grow in branches.
Water engineers design pipe networks with equal path lengths, like the H-tree, to deliver water or signals to many places at the same time.
Chip designers use H-tree layouts to deliver the clock signal to every part of a processor at the same time.

open_questions.q: Why do so many plants use turns close to the golden angle?
open_questions.why_open: The packing idea and the growing tip idea both fit the evidence. Scientists are still working out how they fit together, and some plants do not follow the pattern at all.

open_questions.q: How do the spiral arms of a galaxy last for billions of years?
open_questions.why_open: The density wave idea is one explanation, and other ideas suggest that arms come and go. Observations of other galaxies and computer models are still being compared.

open_questions.q: Do animals such as leopards and zebras form their spots and stripes by a Turing process?
open_questions.why_open: Turing patterns are supported in a few animals, but in most the chemicals have not been found.

open_questions.q: How does a snail's body set the fraction by which each new coil is wider?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the genes involved in a few cases of the direction of coiling, but how the rate of widening is set is less clear.

open_questions.q: Is a coast really a fractal, or is the idea only a convenient description?
open_questions.why_open: Coasts are rough over a range of sizes, but the measured number changes with the range and the method, and mathematicians disagree about how much it means.

open_questions.q: Which other natural branching patterns follow Leonardo's rule or Murray's law, and why?
open_questions.why_open: The rules fit many trees and vessels, but explanations differ and some plants and animals do not follow them closely.

maths.problem: A Koch curve starts as a line 27 centimetres long. Each round multiplies the length by 4 over 3. After how many rounds is the curve first longer than 100 centimetres?
maths.explain: The lengths are 36, 48, 64, about 85 and about 114 centimetres after rounds 1 to 5. Round 4 is 85, which is still less than 100. Round 5 is the first over 100.
maths.context: In the Koch curve activity, you drew a line that grew by 4 over 3 each round.
maths.why_maths: Repeating a multiplication shows how a small step grows into a large length.

maths.problem: Box counts for a drawn coast were 11, 27 and 64 boxes for boxes of 4, 2 and 1 centimetres. What are the two ratios, and what roughness number does their middle give, using the table: 2.4 gives 1.3, 2.6 gives 1.4?
maths.answer: 27 divided by 11 is about 2.45, and 64 divided by 27 is about 2.37. The middle is about 2.4, so the roughness number is about 1.3.
maths.explain: 27 divided by 11 is 2.45 and 64 divided by 27 is 2.37. The middle of the two is about 2.4. The table gives a roughness number of 1.3 for a ratio of 2.4.
maths.context: In the box counting test, you counted the boxes your coast touched at three box sizes and divided the counts.
maths.why_maths: A ratio of counts is a single number that tells you how fast the count grows, and so how rough the line is.

maths.problem: A plant turns 3 over 8 of a circle from one leaf to the next, which is 135 degrees. How many degrees has the stem turned from leaf 0 to leaf 8? How many whole turns is that?
maths.explain: 8 times 135 is 1080. A whole turn is 360 degrees, and 1080 divided by 360 is 3. So leaf 8 sits directly above leaf 0 after 3 turns.
maths.context: In the Leaf Staircase test, you found the leaf directly above the first and counted the turns.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the angle per leaf by the number of leaves checks whether the leaf lands directly above the first.

maths.problem: Plant A turns 2 over 5 of a circle between leaves. Plant B turns 3 over 8. Which turns more between leaves? Compare the fractions and then the angles.
maths.answer: Plant A turns more. 2 over 5 is 144 degrees and 3 over 8 is 135 degrees.
maths.explain: As fractions with a common bottom of 40, 2 over 5 is 16 over 40 and 3 over 8 is 15 over 40. 16 is more than 15. In degrees, 144 is more than 135.
maths.context: In the Leaf Staircase test, you worked out the fraction of a turn for each plant.
maths.why_maths: Comparing fractions tells you which plant spaces the leaves further round, without measuring angles.

maths.problem: The whorls of a shell are 20 millimetres and 30 millimetres wide, and the ratio between neighbouring whorls stays the same. How wide are the next two bigger whorls?
maths.explain: The ratio is 30 divided by 20, which is 1.5. The next whorl is 30 times 1.5, which is 45. The one after is 45 times 1.5, which is 67.5.
maths.context: In the Equal Gaps or Growing Gaps activity, you divided neighbouring whorl widths to find a ratio.
maths.why_maths: Once you know the ratio, multiplying finds the next whorl and dividing finds the one before.

maths.problem: A paper strip is folded in half and opened, and has 1 crease after one fold, 3 after two, 7 after three and 15 after four. How many creases after ten folds?
maths.explain: After n folds there are 2 multiplied by itself n times, minus 1. For 10 folds, 2 multiplied 10 times is 1024. Subtracting 1 gives 1023.
maths.context: In the Fold a Dragon activity, you counted the creases after different numbers of folds.
maths.why_maths: Finding the pattern in the first few counts lets you predict a count that is too big to fold.

maths.problem: Maha rolled a die 60 times for the Chaos Game. Corner A came up 26 times, corner B 15 times and corner C 19 times. About how many times would you expect each corner? Does the result show the die is unfair?
maths.answer: About 20 times each. No, the difference is common with a fair die.
maths.explain: A fair die sends the dot to each corner a third of the time, so 60 divided by 3 is 20. Counts of 26, 15 and 19 are all a few away from 20. Such differences happen often by chance, so 60 rolls are too few to say the die is unfair.
maths.context: In the Chaos Game, a die chose the corner for each dot.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how far chance can stray from the expected count tells you when a result is odd enough to investigate.

maths.problem: In the H-tree for 16 pots, the pipes are 2 pieces of 2 squares, 4 pieces of 2 squares, 8 pieces of 1 square and 16 pieces of 1 square. Each square stands for 15 centimetres. How long is the whole network in metres and centimetres, and how far is each pot from the tap?
maths.answer: The network is 36 squares, which is 540 centimetres, or 5 metres 40 centimetres. Each pot is 6 squares, or 90 centimetres, from the tap.
maths.explain: 2 pieces of 2 squares is 4, 4 pieces of 2 squares is 8, 8 pieces of 1 square is 8 and 16 pieces of 1 square is 16. 4 plus 8 plus 8 plus 16 is 36 squares. 36 times 15 is 540 centimetres. The path to each pot is 2 plus 2 plus 1 plus 1, which is 6 squares, and 6 times 15 is 90 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Water for Every Pot challenge, you drew an H-shaped pipe network and added up the pipe.
maths.why_maths: Adding the pipe lengths and changing squares to centimetres tells you how much pipe to buy.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1800s, mathematicians believed that every curve they could draw was smooth enough to have a direction at almost every point, like a road with a bend here and there. In 1872, the German mathematician Karl Weierstrass showed a curve with no direction at any point. It was made of bends inside bends at every size. Some mathematicians were upset and called such curves monsters. In 1904, the Swedish mathematician Helge von Koch drew a simpler monster that anyone can make with a ruler, which we now call the Koch curve. For decades the monsters stayed in mathematics books. Then, in the 1960s and 1970s, Benoit Mandelbrot used Lewis Fry Richardson's measurements of coasts and argued that the monsters were the right shapes for coasts, clouds and mountains. In 1975, he gave them the name fractals.
how_we_found_out.who: Karl Weierstrass, Helge von Koch and Benoit Mandelbrot
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Mathematicians believed that every curve is smooth enough to have a direction at nearly every point, so that crinkly curves were rare oddities. Weierstrass and Koch showed that a curve can be crinkly everywhere, and Mandelbrot argued that nature is full of such curves.

playtest: Walked through as a parent and child in a city flat would do it, but not yet tried at home. Box counting: a hand-drawn coast on 1 centimetre squared paper with bays inside bays is expected to give a ratio of about 2.2 to 2.8 when the boxes are halved, which is a roughness number of about 1.1 to 1.5. A line drawn through the middle of a row of squares touches 20 boxes of 1 centimetre. The 4 centimetre grid has 5 boxes across a 20 centimetre page. Leaf Staircase: needs a plant with leaves arranged one at a time. Stems lean and leaves are never exactly above one another, so choose the nearest and count twice. Results of 1 over 2, 1 over 3, 2 over 5 and 3 over 8 are all good results. Koch curve: 27 centimetres gives 36, 48, 64 and about 85 centimetres, and round 2 has 4 small tents of 3 centimetres to draw. Dragon: stop at four folds, because five folds of paper is too thick. Chaos game: after 50 dots a clear hole in the middle appears, and 100 dots show it better. Stick and Wander: about 14 rolls per walker on a 7 by 7 grid, tested by computer simulation.
